After making obeisance to the self-born god Brahma, Hiranyagarbha (a golden-fetus, born of golden egg), who is the lord, is the first and the last Purusa, who is the distinguished and superior Atman of the subjects and who governs the worlds, I shall relate in details the excellent creation without leaving anything in doubt. The creation starts with the principle of Mahal and ends with Visesa{ the gross body). 2 It is describ¬ ed in diversity of forms and characteristics with the five dimen¬ sions and six (dividing?) systems. 4.15: It is devoid of smell, colour, taste, sound and touch. It is unborn, steady, imperishable, eternal and stationed in its own Atman. It is the origin of the universe. It is the great Being, the great Brahman, the eternal. It is unmanifest and is indeed the extension of all elements.
4.16: It is beginningless, endless, unborn, subtle, possessed of three attributes. It is the source and the immutable one. This timeless (lit. not belonging to the present), incomprehensible. Brahman was in the beginning.

4.19: It is born of the subtle mind, presided over by the in¬ telligent consciousness. Dharma etc. and their various forms are the causes of the ingredients of creation. When urged by desire to create, the principle of Mahat performs the creation. The terms Manas, Mahat, Mali, Brahma, Puh, Buddhi, Khyati, livara, Prajha, Citi, Smrti, Samvit, and Vipura are synony¬ mous, 1 so say the learned people.
4.20: Since it conceives of the fruit of the activities that multiply in a subtle way, it is called Manas.
4.21: It is termed as Mahat because it is born ahead of all the principles and is greater in dimension than other principles and attributes. It is called Mali because it bears (comprehends) the measure, thinks of the division and is considered to be the Purusa in view of its relationship in enjoyment.
4.22: It is (etymologically) designated as Brahman be¬ cause of its bigness and because it creates the beings and lifts them up from their resting place, the cosmic water.

4.25: It is proclaimed by its attributes and is known by differ¬ ent names. Hcnc cKhyali has been the epithet of Mahat. Since it knows everything directly, it is called the noble- souled favara. It is called Prajhd because organs of perception are born of it.
4.26: It is called Citi because it collects the forms, knowledge etc. and the fruits of sacrificial rites for enjoyment.
4.27: It is declared as Smrti because it is mindful of all acti¬ vities and affects present, past and future. It is called Samvii (derived either from 's/vid or 's/vind) as it obtains complete knowledge and hence its greatness.
4.28: It exists in everything and everything exists in it. Hence it is termed as Samvit by the ones possessing higher intelligence.
4.29: That receptacle of knowledge, (the omniscient) lord, proclaimed that knowledge arises from knowledge, Mahat is called Vipura by the learned because the Dvandvas (mutually clashing pairs) are covered by it. Because of its being absolute controller of all worlds, it is called Isvaran. It is called Brahman because of its bigness. It is Bhava because of its existence.

4.31: The first excellent Tattva ( Mahat ) has been thus explain¬ ed through synonymous words by the knowers of truth and those who meditate on reality. Urged by the desire for creation, Mahat performs crea¬ tion. Its two-fold activities are conception and exertion.
4.32: Dharma and other principles are the ingredients of creation. Mahat is three-fold by virtue of the three gunas y viz. sattva, rajas and tamas.
4.33: From Mahat of threefold Gunas, is born Ego when the rajoguna is predominant. The creation of Ego is secondary and is enveloped by Mahat. Thereafter, when the (cosmic) Ego is dominated by tamas-gima, the primary subtle element is born of the Ego char¬ acterized by lamas.
4.34: Ether is a perforated (void) extensive expanse and is characterized by the subtle element called sound and is again enveloped by the cosmic Ego ( Bhutadi ).
4.35: It is reported that ether characterised by the subtle element sound created the subtle element touch. The Ego under¬ going a change created the subtle element sound. Ether characterised by its subtle element of sound enveloped the subtle element of touch.

6.7: Ekarnava, 'the primeval watery flood' expresses the infinite unmanifest cause of the universe. Nilakantha on HV. P. 3. 9. 1-4 calls it the Kararia Brahman from which all life comes into being. Puranas believe in this doctrine and -use ■ Maharnava y agddha, stabdha, salila (HV. 3. 10. 1), Yuganta-toya 'Water flood at the end of Yuga' (Bh. P. III. 8. 23) as synonyms for Ekarnava. This doctrine is very old and Brahma-Vadins (expounders of Vedas) have elaborated it to explain the process of creation and dissolution (VP. I. 2. 22 ).
6.8: The usual derivation of Narayana in other Puranas also. But Bd. P. I. 4. 27 traces it to Nara: Brahma causes the sleep (i.e. perfect rest) of Naras (men), hence he is remembered as Narayana.

6.10: Observing that the earth was overflowed with waters on all sides, (he thought to himself), cc Oh, what great form should I assume and uplift the earth?"
6.11: He thought of the form of a Boar 1 charmingly comfor¬ table in sporting about in waters. It was unassailable by living beings. It was of the nature of speech and was dcsigxiated as Dharma*.
6.12: It hadagirth of ten and a height of a hundred Yojanas. It resembled a dark blue cloud in complexion. It grunted like the rumbling of thunder-clouds. It had a huge body like a mountain. Its curved fangs were white and sharp and terrible. The eyes were brilliant like lightning and fire. Its lustre was like that of the sun.
6.13: Its shoulders were round, plump and large. It had the lion s valiant gait. Its buttocks were stout and lifted up (well developed). It had auspicious characteristics. It was charming.
6.14: Assuming this large immeasurable form of a boar, Visnu entered the nether regions in order to lift up the earth. He was the guide for the propounders of the Vedas. 2
6.15: The day and the night constituted his eyes. The ancill- aries of the Vedas were his ear ornaments. The Ajya (ghee offer¬ ing in sacrifice) was his nose; the sacrificial ladle was his snout. The sound of the Saman hymns was his roaring grunt.
6.16: Endowed with glory as he was, he was an embodiment of truth and dharma and was established in virtuous valour. He was engaged in expiation. He was terrible. He had the huge form with the knees of an animal. His body was straightened up. The offerings of ghrta constituted his Linga (symbol). The (sacrificial) spot was his seed. He was the great medicinal herb (incarnate for curing distress). The altar was his inner soul. Mantras were his hips. The Soma mixed with clarified butter was his blood.
6.17: The Vedas were his shoulders. He had the fragrance of sacrificial offering. The Havya (oblations for the Devas) and Kavya (oblations for the Pitrs) constituted his velocity. PragvamSa 1 (the room accommodating the sacrifices) was his body. He was lustrous and had undergone different initiations.
6.18: The sacrificial fees constituted his heart. He was an all- pervading Yogin in the form of a great Sattva.. He was charm¬ ing with the sacrificial rites of Upakarman. Pravargya (a rite in which hot milk is poured in a vessel, thus giving rise to fumes) constituted the whorls of hair on his chest* 2. His gait and paths were the different Chandas. The secret Upanisads constituted his seat. He was accompanied by his consort Chaya. He was lofty like a jewelled peak. Having thus assumed the form of a sacrificial Boar, the lord entered the waters.
6.19: The body of Varaha was so big and spacious as to accommodate many men, as PragvarhSa (the room in which the members of the sacrificer's family and friends stay) is spacious.
6.20: He, the lord of the subjects, got at the Earth covered with the waters. He approached and lifted it quickly. He divert¬ ed the waters of the oceans in the oceans and of the rivers in the rivers. The lord, for the welfare of the worlds, lifted with his curved fangs, the Earth that had gone deep into the nether world. Holding the Earth in his hands he brought it to its place. The supporter of the Earth at first mentally supported the earth and then released it.
6.21: Over the flood of waters, the Earth floated like an immense boat. Due to the activities of the lord, it did not sink.
6.22: With a desire to set up the universe, the lord lifted up the Earth. Then, he, the lotus-eyed lord, decided to divide the Earth. He levelled the Earth and created the mountains on it. Formerly when the creation was burnt by the Samvar- taka fire, all the mountains, being consumed by that fire, lay shattered and scattered all over the earth.
6.23: In that Ekarijiava (the ocean of cosmic waters) the waters (solidifiedby cold) and collected by wind and were placed in a scattered manner here and there (wherever they were thus deposited); they became condensed into mountains.
6.24: Since they became motionless after being (thus) sprin¬ kled, they were known as Acalas. 1 Since they are endowed with knots and joints, they were called Parvalas. Since they had been swallowed and hidden (formerly), they were called Giris. Since they had heen collected, they were called Siloccayas. Thus after the worlds, oceans and mountains are des¬ troyed at the end of a Kalpa, the Maker (Creator) of the uni¬ verse creates them again and again, in the beginnings of the Kalpas.

6.26: Note the Puranic etymologies of acala, panala, giri. Desirous of creating different species pf subjects, the self-born lord Brahma recreated the beings in the same form as they had in the previous Kalpas. 1
6.27: When he was contemplating over the creation intellec¬ tually, the dark and gloomy creation manifested itself simultane¬ ously with Pradhana.* *
6.28: Nescience ( Avidya ) with five joints, viz. darkness, delusion, super-delusion, murkiness and super-murkiness**, be¬ came manifested out of the Supreme Soul. While he meditated, the creation became established in five ways. Just as a lamp is covered up with a pot, the creation was enveloped by darkness. Like a lamp lighted in a pitcher illuminated within and (dark) without, it was pure but devoid of feeling.
6.29: Its intellect and sense organs were concealed; it consis¬ ted of vegetation and since vegetation is declared to be primary it was called primary creation.
6.30: On seeing that the creation did not multiply, Brahma was dissatisfied and he went into contemplation. When he contemplated thus the Tirjaksrolas (tire animal world) came into being. Since this creation proceeded obliquely, it was called Tirjaksrolas. Predominated by Tamas, they were mainly ignorant. They took to wrong direction. They were self-swayed and devoted to self.
6.31: The lord saw this second creation of Tiiyak-srotas, proud of themselves, conceited and divided into twenty-eight— eleven based on the sense organs, nine of Udaya and the eight of Taraka and other Saktis.
6.32: Puranas believe that despite the annihilation of everything at the end of a Kalpa, god Brahma recreates the universe on the model of the previous universe. They state this succinctly as follows: dhata yathopunam akalpayat' They were all illuminated within but covered exter¬ nally. Since their activity was oblique, they were called Tiryak- srotas.
6.33: Having seen the second universe, the Tiryaksrotas, and having observed everything of it of that designation (nature), the Lord conceived of the (following) idea: Even as he was thinking uninterruptedly (nilyam), the Sattvika creation appeared (ofitself, automatically).
6.34: This third creation was called Ordhvasrotas, consisting of beings in which the stream of life passed upwards. Since life proceeded upwards it was called Ordhvasroias. The Ordhvasroias beings have abundance of comfort and pleasure. They are circumscribed outwardly and inwardly and are brilliant externally and internally.
6.35: These created beings are air etc. They are well settled after creating themselves. The Ordhvasroias being the third (in the series of creations), that creation is known after them.
6.36: When gods with.upward stream (the divine creation of Ordhvasroias) were created god Brahma was satisfied. As he was the competent Over-Lord, he thought of and created beings that would be Sadhakas (aspirants after spiritual power). The first creation is of Mahal. It is known as Mahat- sarga. 6.37: The third creation is that of Vikaras (the products of Prakfti) and is perceptible by the senses. Thus the Prakrta creation took place with conscious fore-knowledge.
6.38: The ' Mukhya' creation is the fourth in order. The Muk- hyas are the immobile beings. The creation of Tiryaksrolas is the fifth consisting of animals. The sixth creation of Ord/wasrotas consists of divine beings. The seventh creation of the Arvdksrolas is that of man¬ kind.
6.39: The eighth creation is Aimgraha. It is characterised by Sattva and Tamas. These (latter) five are the Vaikrla creation and the (first) three are Prakrta.
6.40: The ninth creation Kaumdra is both Prakrta and Vaikrla. The three Prakrta creations were brought about with¬ out planning or pre-meditation. The six creations of Brahma function intelligently. Now understand the Anugraha Sarga in detail. It is of four types found in all living beings thro¬ ugh contrariety, power, satisfaction and achievement. In the immobile beings there is Viparyasa (contrariety or loss of con¬ sciousness). In the animals, there is Sakli (power). Human be¬ ings are Siddhatmans (with souls capable of achieving spiritual progress). In Devas there is Tusti (satisfaction).
6.41: There are thus the nine creations including Prakrtas and Vaikrlas. By their mutual combination, the types are many.

6.43: They are water, fire, earth, air, ether, quarters, heaven, firmament, oceans, rivers, mountains, plants, the 'souls' of medicinal herbs, trees and creepers, units of time, Lavas, Kas- ihas, A aids, Muhurtas, Sandhis (junctions of day and night like dusk, dawn etc.), night, day, fortnights, months, Ay anas, years and Yugas. These arc the positions with which they identify themselves.

The lord is beyond Avyakla (unmanifest Prakrti). The Cosmic Egg is born of the unmanifest. Brahma is born of the Cosmic Egg. The worlds are created by him.

7.3: O sages of holy rites, now understand the Manvan- taras that are in the Kalpas. This auspicious Kalpa that is current now is (called the) Varaha Kalpa. The Kalpa that has gone before this Kalpa was (known as) Sana tana. Now understand the (condition of) the interim period between that Kalpa and the present one. Out of the five main characteristics of a Purana, description of Man- vantaras is one. Thus we find it in Bh. P. VIII. 1. 1-29, KP. I. 51, NP. I. 40. 17-37 and others. This chapter which textually corresponds to Bd. P. I. 2. 6 deals with Kalpas and the interim period between them.
7.4: When the previous Kalpa recedes there is a period of transition. Another Kalpa sets in again and again from Jana- loka. This happens again and again when the period of transi¬ tion ends, the Kalpas are cut off from each other. At the end of a Kalpa, all the rites are completely annihilated. Hence it is called the period of transition between one Kalpa and another. The joints (transition) between the periods called Man- vantara and Yuga are also cut off. Manvantaras function with the inter-connectionsof Yugas.

The Kalpa that is current, O Brahmanas, is the first among them.

Verses 44-63 paint a glowing picture of the Krta age. They depict the ideal state of society from Puraijic point of view—a classless society with perfect equality and full liberty. The people in that age resorted to rivers, lakes, oceans and mountains. The waters in that Yuga were neither too hot nor too cold.
8.15: They usually took the diet of the juicy food of the earth. They moved about wherever they pleased. They had acquired mental Siddhis. In that Krta age, there was neither virtue nor evil. The human beings were non-differentiated. They had equal longevity, happiness and beauty (form). In the beginning of the Kalpa, in the Krta age, neither virtue (Dharma) nor evil (Adharma) existed. The people were born with their respective authority and rights.
8.16: The first Krta age consisted of four thousand divine Even when thousands of human beings spread they had no obstruction, no clash and no order. They had no fixed abode or place of resort. They wandered about mountains and oceans. They were free from sorrow. They had abundant goodness. They were happy in solitude.
8.17: They moved about as they pleased. They were always joyous in their minds. There were no animals, birds or reptiles then. There were no trees or plants nor hellish beings born of evil. There were neither roots nor fruits nor flowers nor the seasons nor the years. Time was always pleasant when peoples' desires were fulfilled. There were no extremes in heat or cold. Whatever object they desired in their minds was available everywhere and at all times.
8.18: Whatever juices they meditated upon, grew up from the earth. Their achievements were conducive to strength, fair complexion and destructive of ailments. With their bodies requiring no decoration (or beauti¬ fication), the subjects had eternal youth. Pairs of children were born from their pure mental conception. They were born alike and they died together. They had similar forms and features. At that time, there was truth, absence of greed, forbearance, contentment, happiness and restraint.
8.19: They had no distinguishing marks in their forms and features, longevity, conduct and activity. Their actions were spontaneous and voluntary, without the intercession of intellect. In the Krtavuga, there was no inclination towards performance, of good or evil actions. There was no classification of castes or differentiation in stages of life. Nor was there inter¬ mixture of castes. In their mutual dealings they behaved without being impelled by desire or hatred. All of them, had equal forms, features and longevity. There was neither superior nor inferior class of people.
8.20: Only those who were mostly happy and devoid of sorrow were born in the Krta Yuga. They were highly power¬ ful, very strong and perpetually delighted in the mind. They had neither gain nor loss; neither friends nor foes; neither likes nor dislikes, since they were devoid of desires. The objects functioned according to their minds. They neither desired to possess nor favoured one another. It has been said that in the Krta age meditation was the highest; in Treta it was knowledge; in Dvapara it was sacrifice, while charity (donation) is excellent m Kali age.

The characteristic duties of a Brahmacarin are: (bear¬ ing) the staff, wearing the girdle (of muhja grass), sleeping on the bare ground, having matted hair, service to the preceptor and begging alms. Wearing of bark garments, leaves or deer skin, diet of grains, roots, fruits or herbs (found in the forest), bathing at dawn and dusk and performing sacrifice are the characteristics of a forest-dweller.

Sanat continues to have the same form and features as at the time of his birth. So he is called Kumara. Hence his name is mentioned Sanatkumara.
9.50: Their twelve races are divine and endowed with divine attributes. Performing holy rites and multiplying the race, they are embellished by great sages. Thus ends (the description of) the activity of the self-born lord in creating the worlds. The creation was born of his various organs. The creation beginning with Mahat and ending with ViSesas belongs to Prakrli itself.
9.51: The light of the sun and the moon illuminates the world which is further embellished with planets and stars. It is surrounded by rivers, oceans, mountains, and cities of various shapes and sizes, and happy countryside. In that unmanifest Brnhmavana, Brahma spends the night. This eternal tree of Brahma is born of the seed of Avyakla. It grows up through his blessings. Intellect constitutes its branches and the sense-organs its sprout and Dharma and Adharma its flowers, happiness and sorrow its fruits. It is the source of livelihood for living beings and its root is Brahman.
9.52: The unmanifest which is the cause of creation is eternal and of the nature of Sat and Asal. This is the Anugraha Sarga, the primary creation of Brahma. The six creations Mukhya etc. are secondary. They exist in all the three times in Brahma who identifies with them.
9.53: It is known by the learned that the creations fun¬ ction as causes of one another. There are two divine trees growing together, having fine leaves and sprouts and branches. Only one knows the tree of the Atman and not the other. That incomprehensible Atman is the cause of creation of all living beings—he whose head the Brahmanas eulogise as heaven; the sky as the umbilicus; the sun and the moon as the eyes; the quarters as the ears; and the earth as his feet.
9.54: From his mouth the Brahmanas were born; from his arms the Ksatriyas; from his thigh the Vaisyas and from his The great lord is beyond the unmamfest. The cosmic Egg is born of the unmanifest. From the cosmic Egg is born Brahma who created the universe.
9.55: An echo of RV X. 90 (Purusa Sukta).

12.2: But even though one has mastered breath-control and evils (obstructing Yoga), other evils arising from (and of the nature of) Sattva, Rajas and Tamas appear. Covering himself with a white cloth or a blanket he should quickly meditate upon the great Brahman.
12.7: If the inelligent Yogi desires to attain his spiritual power, he should give up (overcome) his defects caused by the (spiritual) disturbances. Devas, Gandharvas, Sages, Yaksas, Serpents and Asuras, that are involved in creating obstruction, come again and again.
12.8: A practising Yogin should always take light food and subdue the sense-organs. Similarly he should lie and repose in the subtle body and perform Dharana in the head. Then, if he conquers sleep after practising Yoga, Upasargas in the form of vital breaths are produced in the end.
12.9: He should then perform Dharanas of the earth, waters, fire, ether and the mind. Then the striving (aspiring) recluse should perform Dharana upon his intellect. He should discard instantly whenever he sees the indications of (coming) Siddhis.
12.10: While he performs the Dharana of the earth, the earth becomes subtle. While he performs the Dharana of waters, the waters become subtle. Cool juices, subtle and nectar-like, begin to function. While he performs the Dharana of fire, the subtle fire begins to function. He feels himself like fire and sees its subtle nature.
12.11: He considers himself to be wind and the universal sphere as made of that*. While he performs the Dharana of the ether, the subtle ether begins to function. He sees its subtle sphere and its sound begins to function. The Yogin who, after knowing the seven subtle elements abandons them, attains the highest point of intellect.
12.12: If he identifies with any of these elements characterised by Aisvarya (prosperity or mastery), he becomes entangled and thereby perishes. Hence he who knows the subtle elements attached to one another and abandons them deliberately, attains the supreme lord.
12.13: Indeed, even the noble-souled sages of divine vision are found entangled in the subtle elements. Those are regarded as defects in them. Hence no attachment should be had in regard to the subtle elements. Due to AUvarya (prosperity and glory) attach¬ ment is generated, while Brahman is called non-attached.
12.14: After knowing the seven subtle (elements etc.) and the excellent great god of six characteristics, he attains to the supreme Brahman. Those who know the procedure, declare the (following) six characteristics of the supreme Lord. These are: omniscience, contentment, beginning-less (external knowledge), independence, never-failing power and infinite power.
12.15: The practising Yogin with Brahman as his permanent asset, becomes liberated from the Upasargas. To a Yogin who has conquered the vital breath, the Upasargas and passion, there remains only one Dharana inclusive of all desires in the external body. When the twice-born fixes his mind anywhere he enters it. He enters the elements and can.even shake (move) the three worlds.
12.16: Be means of this Dharana, he can abandon his body and enter another. He should determine that the Sun is e mental door of the Yoga. The Yogin who has attained the status of Isvara and Gunas becomes Brahman himself. He withdraws himse rom the positions of Devas.

13.1: The eightfold AiSvarya too functions in the' subtle elements. I shall explain its features as the lord has described.
13.2: In all the three worlds, among all living beings, the power of Anima (becoming minute like an atom) is uncontrolled. It is unmanifest. It is the basis of all (powers).
13.3: What is stated to be inaccessible to living beings in the three worlds becomes accessible to the Yogins by virtue of this first power.
13.4: The second power in Yoga consists of descending (hanging down) and floating. The Yogi possessed of thispower can move the fastest in all beings.
13.5: The ability to obtain anything in the three worlds is called Prakamya (irresistible will). *What is Mahima also falls under this category. This is the third Yoga (Yogic power).
13.6: These three worlds are regarded as untraversable to ail beings (except Yogins) in the three w.orlds. It is theYogin who can enjoy all objects to the utmost satisfaction. He is not obstructed anywhere. Happiness and misery befall all living beings in the three worlds (but the Yogin escapes).
13.7: The Yogin becomes the lord of everything. In the three worlds including the mobile and immobile beings the living beings become submissive to him. They can be made to serve if he so wishes, not otherwise.
13.8: Where there is the supernormal power called Kamava - sdyitva, by the mere will (of the Yogi), the sense-organs function or do not function according to his will.
13.9: Objects of senses, viz. Sound, Touch, Taste, Smell and Colour as well as the mind function or do not function just in compliance of his will.
13.10: He is neither born nor does he die. He is neither broken nor cut. He does not get burnt nor does he lose his sense. He is neither deficient nor attached.
13.11: He does not get diminished or waste away. He does not perish. He is never dejected. Anywhere he can do anything or undo it.
13.12: He is not characterised by smell, taste, colour, touch and sound. He is castcless, but not inferior to any caste.
13.13: He enjoys sensual objects but is not entangled by them. On realising the greatest and die subtlest Brahman, because of his subtlety, he attains salvation.
13.14: Because of salvation, he becomes all-pervading. Be¬ cause he pervades (everything), he is called Purus a. Due to his subtle form, the Purusa is established in Supremacy.
13.15: Another characteristic of his Supremacy is the all¬ round subtlety. After attaining the most excellent Yoga, of unobstructed supremacy, he goes to the subtlest region, the state of Liberation.

14.1: A person who has come thus (to this stage) due to knowledge,.should not perform any action due to passion. After experiencing the Rajasic and Tamasic fruits, he becomes attached there.
14.2: Similarly the man who has performed meritorious actions enjoys the fruits in heaven. Fallen from that region, he is born again as a human being.
14.3: Brahman is therefore, supreme and subtle. Brahman is. said to be eternal. One should devote oneself to Brahman as Brahman is the supreme bliss.
14.4: There is great exertion in performing sacrifice requiring great deal of (expenditure of) wealth. Moreover he (the sacrificer) is subject to death. Salvation therefore is the greatest bliss.
14.5: But he who is engaged in meditation and devoted to the sacrifice of Brahman cannot be reached even in hundreds of Manvantaras.
14.6: He visualizes the divine Purusa that is called the Vtiva (all-pervading). He appears in various forms. He has feet, heads and necks everywhere (pervades the Universe). He is the Lord and the creator of the Universe. He has the cosmic fragrance, is garlanded cosmically and robed in cosmic apparel. He is the Ruler of all.
14.7: By means of their sense-organs people endeavour to visualize him who is the winged noble soul, the most excellent and the greatest Soul. But it is not with the eyes but with the mental concentration called Yoga that they can see the omni¬ scient, ancient governor (Teacher) who is subtler than the subt¬ lest, greater than the greatest, the Purusa of golden complexion, devoid of sense-organs.
14.8: They always see Purusa who is golden in colour, en¬ dowed with or without exterior symbols, devoid of attributes, conscious, eternal, all-pervading and pure. By means of Yoga, they see the steady light.
14.9: Manifested thereby He shines in his own refulgence. He is devoid of heads, feet, belly, sides and tongue, but he, though beyond the ken of senses, though still extremely subtle and alone, can see without eyes and hear without ears.
14.10: There is nothing that is not known to him; yet he has no intellect. He knows all, yet he is not known to the Vedas. They call him the foremost or the first Purusa, the great, the sentient, all-pervading and very subtle.
14.11: All sages call that Prakrti, which gives birth to living beings in this world. Those who are engaged in Yoga, can visualize it mentally.
14.12: Those who are engaged in Yogic meditation on the eternal Purusa who is endowed with hands and feet, eyes, heads and faces (mouths), ears on all sides and who stays after permeating everything in the world (who is both immanent and transcendent) and who governs everything, does not become deluded.
14.13: One does not get deluded after meditating on the supreme Brahman, the Soul of all living beings, the imperish¬ able, noble, supreme soul, the soul of all.
14.14: Just as the (presence of the) wind is to be admitted as evident through its movement in clouds, so is that of the Atman that moves through the bodies of all. Since the Soul abides in the body, it is named Purusa. When the merit is ex¬ hausted due to specific Karmans he is born and re-born in the womb by the mixture of semen and blood as a result of the mixture of male and female flesh. 1
14.15: Then, at the time of conception, Kalana, the embryo at its first stage (in the form of a drop) is formed. In due course the Kalana develops into bubbles.
14.16: Just as a lump of clay pressed by the wind in the potter's wheel and shaped by the hands (of the potter) attains multifarious shapes, so also the foetus united with bones and impelled by the wind becomes a human body with proper forms, features and mind.
14.17: The wind assembles them together. From the wind water is generated. From the water the vital breath is formed and through the vital breath the semen gets developed.
14.18: The child in the womb is covered by the five vital breaths. From the father's body he inherits his forms and features..
14.19: The food of the mother, drunk or licked, enters through the umbilical cord and sustains the foetus in the womb.
14.20: For nine months the child suffers in the body with his neck encircled by the inner vessels of its mother. His limbs are covered in disorder. He remains there for nine months. He then comes out through the vaginal passage with the head downwards.
14.21: Then (in his life on the earth) he commits some sinful actions and as a result he goes to the hell (after death), Asipatravana or Salmali where he is cut or pierced. 2
14.22: Verses 16-25 give Purajiic (Mediaeval) ideas on Embryology.
14.23: Verses 25-31 describe the tortures in hell.
14.24: In the hell, he is rebuked and threatened. He is forced to drink blood. These are the terrible tortures he has to undergo in Kumbhipaka. They are very unbearable.
14.25: Just as waters though parted regain their normal form, so also the hellish beings though cut and broken in torturing hells regain their original form.
14.26: Thus the living beings become agitated and tortured through their own sins. If there is anything left over, they take other, births.
14.27: Man must go alone to the abode of death. He must bear the punishments alone. Hence one should perform pious deeds.
14.28: None follows him who proceeds along the path of death. But the actions performed by him pursue him.
14.29: The hellish beings always cry in the abode of Yama when they are pierced or when tortures are inflicted on their bodies. Their bodies being tortured get withered up and suffer extreme pain caused by evil harassments.
14.30: The sin may forcibly remove everything desirable re¬ sorted to by him mentally, verbally or physically. Hence one should perform meritorious deeds.
14.31: In accordance with the sinful actions committed by him previously, the embodied being undergoes six types of worldly transmigrations of Tdmasa nature. 1
14.32: They are: Birth as human beings; as domestic animals (Pa$u); from the state of Pastt (he becomes) a wild animal; from that stage (he goes to) the birds; from 'bird-hood* to reptiles; from reptilehood he certainly becomes an immobile. He who has attained the immobile state evolves into a human being. He thus rotates like one propelled by the potter's wheel.
14.33: Thus in this migration six types of birth beginning with that as man and ending with that as plant are known as Tamasa. He undergoes many changes there.
14.34: The life in hell and evolution through six stages upto that of man show the acceptance of the principle of redemption. No sinner is condemned to eternal hell.
14.35: The transmigrations beginning.with Brahma and end¬ ing with Pifaca are known as Sattvika. Only in the celestial regions the embodied beings experience these.

16.1: Henceforth I shall explain the characteristics of purity and conduct of life, the observance of which purifies the Atman and leads a person to heaven after death.
16.2: Seeking of water for purity is the excellent state of sages. He who is not negligent in regard to these comes to no trou¬ ble.
16.3: Insult and honour, they say, constitute (what is called) poison and nectar. Insult is poison; honour is nectar.
16.4: The sage who does not err in regard to these comes to no trouble. He should remain with the preceptor for a year enga¬ ged in what is pleasing and beneficial to him.
16.5: He should not be negligent in the observance of vows, major ( Tamas ) or minor ( Niyamas ). After attaining supreme knowledge, he should seek permission from his preceptor and move about the earth consistently with Dharma.
16.6: This is the holy dictate of Dharma, viz. one should go along the path purified by (i.e. observed carefully by) the eyes; one should drink water filtered with a cloth; and one should utter words purified by truth i.e. state the truth only. 2
16.7: It is the considered opinion that the knower of Yoga should never accept hospitality in Sraddhas and Tajnas and that it is only thus that a Yogin becomes non-violent.

16.13: First of all, he should go to the houses of only those householders who maintain good conduct. Such begging for alms is said to be an excellent means of livelihood advised to the Yogin.
16.14: Secondly, he should go to the abodes of modest house¬ holders who arc faithful, self-controlled, learned and noble.
16.15: Last of all he should go to the residence of non-defiled and unfallen people. Begging for alms in the abodes of lower caste is considered mean.
16.16: The alms received may be gruel, butter-milk, milk, barley-water, cooked or uncooked fruits, roots, oil-cake or any¬ thing offered in accordance with the householder's ability.
16.17: Thus the foodstuffs conducive to the increase in Siddhis of Yogins have been proclaimed by me. Among these the most excellent is that which is received by way of alms.
16.18: He who begs alms in a righteous manner, is better than the person who drinks a drop of water from the tip of the hu$a grass once in a month.
16.19: The observance of the Candrayaiia 1 vow is the most ex¬ cellent for the Yogin. He should perform it once, twice, thrice, four times successively or as many times as he can.

16.21: Just as an elephant is caught in the forest, is then controlled, so man with the seeds (of Karmas) as his source of birth, body as gwias, is bound by Karmas. Soon he is trapped and is disciplined like a (wild) elephant. In this way, with the seeds of his Karmas having been burnt by the fire of pure know¬ ledge, He becomes free from bondage and quiescent. He is called the liberated (soul).
16.22: By Vedas, by means of eulogies, all rites in a sacrifice (are pei formed). Jap a is regarded more important than know¬ ledge. Meditation free from association with attachment is better than Juana. When that is achieved, the eternal (Moksa) is obtained.

17.1: He who wanders remaining satisfied with the discrimina¬ tion between knowledge and the knowable, will never attain the knowable even if he were to live for a thousand Kal- pas.
17.2: Giving up contacts and attachment, subduing one's wrath¬ fulness, subsisting on light food, he, with his sense-organs con¬ trolled, should close down all the portals of his intellect and should thus fix his mind in meditation.
17.3: He should always practise Yoga in uninhabited places, caves, forests or on the banks (sands) of rivers. 1
17.4: He who has control over his speech, action and mind and represents each by a long staff is declared as Tridandin 2

18.1: Henceforth I shall explain decisively the expiations pres¬ cribed for ascetics for their (evil) actions done by them ion- Vaikhanasa Sutra VIII. 9 prescribes this for a Paramahamsa. Bud¬ dhist and Jaina mendicants have similar instructions.
18.2: Sin is proclaimed as threefold, according as it is born of (results from) speech, mind and body both by day or night continuously. By this the whole world is bound. The great Sruti declares that no man can stay without activities. In life every moment has to be spent in activity 1 for its sustenance.
18.3: One shall be self-possessed and un-erring. Yoga is the greatest strength. There is nothing seen to be greater than Yoga for men here. Hence, the wise who are endowed with piety praise Yoga. Intelligent and resolute men transcending ignorance through knowledge, attain excellent AiSvarya. Having discrim¬ inated between the greater and the lesser, they attain the highest region.
18.4: Expiation is prescribed for the violation of any major or minor vow ordained for the mendicant. If he approaches a woman cut of lust, the expiation pres¬ cribed is that he shall perform the rite of Sdntapand 2 along with Pranayama.
18.5: He shall follow the prescribed courses (of conduct) at the end of that expiation with mental purity. He should return to the hermitage and move about carefully as a mendicant. The wise people opine that words piercing the heart 3 do not kill (?) However this should not be indulged in. For this results in cruelty.
18.6: Gf.BG III. 5 Santapana is generally prescribed for pollution or falling off from caste ( Jfati-bhramja-kara ). It lasts for two days. One has to take Panca-gavycL on the first day and observe fast on the second day.
18.7: marmayukta is emended as narmayukta jocular remark* in A. The emenda¬ tion deserves consideration. Violence is the greatest of evil deeds created by Devas and sages. What is called wealth is the veritable external life- breath of a man. He who deprives any man of his wealth verily takes away his vital breath (life).
18.8: By committing theft a wicked person shatters off his good conduct. He falls off from his vow. After repenting for this sin, he should perform Candrayana vow for a year in accor¬ dance with the injunctions of the scriptures, says the Sruti. At the end of a year his sin will practically diminish. If he repents again he should vigilantly observe his vow of medicancy. If due to the weakness of his organ, a recluse emits semen on seeing a woman, he should perform sixteen Prana- yamas.
18.9: In the case of a Brahmana who emits semen during day the observance of fast for three nights and performance of a hundred Pranayamai are prescribed for its expiation.
18.10: If he has nocturnal emission of semen, he should take bath and perform twelve Dharanas. He becomes pure in soul and free from sin by performing the Pranayama. Daily eating at the same house, use of honey, flesh and salt as well as feasting at Sraddha are forbidden for the asce- tics.
18.11: For the violation of each of these expiatory rite consist¬ ing of Prajapatya or Krcchra is prescribed. Then alone he becomes free from the sin.

18.13: A Yogin of pure intellect, looking upon a clod of earth and lump of gold alike, behaving with purity of mind toward all livings, attains the region of saintly people which is un¬ shakable, eternal and imperishable. After reaching there he ' not born again (is liberated from Samsara ).

19.3: He who is obstructed by rows of crows or by a dust storm, lives only for four or five months.
19.4: He who sees lightning without clouds, in the southern direction, or water or the rainbow (without the existence of clouds) lives only for two or three months.
19.5: He who does not see his reflection either in water or in a mirror or who sees his reflection without the head does not survive a month.
19.6: If the body smells like a corpse or like burning fat, death is imminent. He lives only for a fortnight.
19.7: If a biting wind seems to pierce the vulnerable points of one's body or if no sensation is experienced after touching water, death is imminent for him.

19.9: If he dreams that he is being led to southern direction by a dark singing woman wearing black garment, he does not survive long.
19.10: If he dreams that he wears black rags or that his ear is broken, it shall be known as a sign of imminent death.

19.12: He who sees (in. dream) ashes, burning coals, hair, dry river and serpents will not survive ten nights.

20.22: [Prose portionj Obeisance to the lord of the world? who has grasped the idea and knowledge of the Kalpas, and whose worship is beneficial to you. Obeisance to the attributeless, eternal Brahman to whom the lord of Yogins is devoted. One should worship him who is extremely pure and unaffected like the lotus-leaf untouched by water. Omkdra is the holiest of holy things. Consisting of syllables short and prolated, it is holy and full of sanctifying things. One shall worship Omkdra devoid of sound, touch, colour, taste and smell. Obeisance to the lord of Prakrti, obeisance to Yoglsvara by whom has been made the fierce firmament, the earth firm and the heaven extended, by whom Elysium has been created and Ether made—the two being the abode of Devas. He has universe as (his) form. He is incomparable with Prana and Apana. He is a sacrifice and constitutes all things. The sacrifice is Veda. Veda is obeisance. Obeisance is Rudra. Hail to Rudra. Obeisance to the lord of the chiefs of Yogins. This prayer for success should be performed in the evening, morning and midday, Rudra bestows the fruits of all desires.

23.2: When the universe was turned into a single vast ocean and a thousand divine years had elapsed, the dejected Brahma desirous of creating the subjects began to think. Then he of great splendour saw that a boy of great powers, dark in complexion and shinning with his lustre had appeared. He wore dark garments, an excellent black turban, black sacred thread, black garlands and unguents and had a black head. On seeing the noble-souled, immortal one with terrible mantras, he (Brahma) paid homage to the dark and tawny Lord of the chief of the Devas and the universe. The glorious Brahma was engaged in Prandydma (breath control). With Maliesvara (the great god) in his heart, he men¬ tally sought refuge in the Lord of ascetics absorbed in medita¬ tion. Brahma then contemplated on Brahman as Aghora. While he was thus meditating Lord Rudra burst out in a boisterous laughter. Then from his sides four noble sons emerged. They were black in complexion and had black garlands and ungu¬ ents. ' They wore black garments, turbans, clothes and had black faces. They laughed aloud boisterously. They uttered great hissing sounds. They performed obeisance again and again. Then they worshipped him for a thousand years by means of Yoga and at the end of that period they transferied their activities to their disciples. Verses 20-32 describe the 32nd Kalpa called Sita (black). Complexion and dress suitable to the name of the Kalpa and birth of four sons a a boistrous laugh—all these are common features to other Avataras of biva. The avatdra or form of Siva here is Aghora.
23.3: Other Brahmanas too well-versed in the injunctions who meditate upon Rudra by means of Yoga attain the eternal lord. When that terrible black Kalpa elapsed, another Kalpa named Visvarupa 1 began to function. After the period of dissolution was over when the mobile and immobile beings were created and when Brahma desirous of sons began to meditate, the omnipresent Sarasvati of great sound manifested (herself). Brahma who had a Yogic communion with his Atman mentally meditated on Isana, the lord of all, the omnipresent, who was clad in universal garlands and robes and who wore universal sacred thread and universal turban and who had applied universal scents, who had mighty arms and had universe as his abode. Brahma bowed to the lord. To him who was thus meditating and saluting, with the words Otii to Isana, O Mahadeva, obeisance be to you," the Lord Isa (Siva) said, "I am pleased with you. Ask what you desire." Then, bowing and eulogising the lord with words, the delighted Brahma replied with a contented mind: O lord I wish to know your universal form that per¬ vades and rules over the universe. I wish to know who is this supreme god. Listen precisely to this holy and nourishing secret of all mantras. It is the great secret of the first creation. The Kalpa that is current now is known as Visvarupa, wherein Devas, Bhava and others and twenty-six Manus (are said to have existed). O Lord, this is the thirty-third Kalpa since you have occupied the position of Brahma.

24.1: When many Manvantaras pass off, the mighty devas of the Kalpa go up and attain Sayujya. When the time of withdrawal (dissolution) arrives, the fourteen Ganas leave Maharloxa. 1 Those gods in combin¬ ation with these (quit the Maharloka), when the elements and immobiles alone are left behind, when all the regions from the Bhuvar-loka to Svar-loka become void; when Devas whose duration of tenure is a Kalpa go upto Janaloka, god Brahma then collects (all) the groups of Devas, sages and Danavas and destroys them all through fire and showers when the Yuga comes to an end. In the seventh Kalpa that has just passed off and has been described to you by me, the seven oceans joined together and formed one vast limitless (and divisionless) ocean full of darkness. In the vast single ocean, the lord holding conch, discus and mace lay on the serpent couch. He had the colour of the cloud. He was lotus-eyed. He had a crown. He was the lord ofLaksmi. He was Hari, the eighth Purusottama born of the mouth of Narayana. He had eight arms, and a broad chest. He is the source of origin of the worlds. He was in communion with the self. Conversant with the process of Yoga, he had taken to meditation beyond the ken of thought, by his Maya. The serpent (his couch) had a thousand hoods; its body had an unparalleled splendour and the lustre of gold. While he was lying there, taking repose in the Atman, he, the mighty Visnu, created a lotus in his umbilicus just for a sport. The lotus extended to a hundred Yojanas. It had the splendour of the midday-sun. It was very high supported by an adamantine stalk. It was created sportively by the powerful lord. Verses 5-14 describe the dissolution of the universe and formation of one ocean (Ekdryana) of cosmic waters with god Visnu lying on the serpent couch and god Brahma born in the lotus-flower blooming on the lotus-plant issuing from Visnu's navel. On hearing the auspicious words of Brahma, Visnu got up from his couch, with eyes outstretched with wonder. 27.12: To the third body of the lord known as Sarva and symbolized by the earth the wife is Vikesi and Ahgaraka (Mars) the son. To the fourth body of the lord known as Isana and symbolized by the wind, the wife is Siva and Manojava the son. The body of Pasuptati which is remembered (procla¬ imed) as Fire by the twice-borns, has Svaha for his wife and Skanda as the son. The ether (Akasa) is called the body Bhima, his sixth name. Quarters are remembered as his wives and Heaven (Svarga) as the son.
27.13: To the seventh body of the Lord known as Ugra and symbolized by the sacrificer, the wife is Diksa (initiation) and Santana as the son. The eighth body of the great Lord is known as the Moon. His wife is Rohini and Budha is remembered as the son. They should be saluted and bowed with respective names to each body. By devotion to these bodies and the names of the Lord, viz. the Sun, the Waters, the Earth, Wind, Fire, Ether, Initiaited Priest and the Moon, the devotee attains Sayujya with the Lord himself. Thus the secret glory of the terrible lord has been narrated to you. Welfare be unto us the bipeds. Welfare be unto our quadrupeds. Thus the origin of the bodies of Lord Mahadeva along with their designations has been recounted. Now listen to progeny of Bhrgu.

28.2: Their eldest sister, the chaste goddess Sri, the purifier of worlds, attained theauspicious lordNarayana as her husband, and gave birth to two sons: Bala (Strength) and Utsaha (Energy).
28.3: Those heaven-walkers who pilot the aerial chariots of Devas and meritorious beings, were born to her as mental sons.
28.4: She had two daughters Ayati and Niyati who are remembered as the wives of Vidhatr and Dhatr. They had two sons Pandu and Mrkandu. They were firm in religious vows, eternal and the very storehouses of the Vedic learning. Mar- kandeya was born of Mrkandu from Manasvinl.

Knowing that her sisters had gone to their father's, Sati, though not invited, went to her father's house. Highly infuriated (with wrath), the goddess spoke to, Daksa: "O Lord! "You are the most excellent of my daughters, foremost and most worthy of my respect for ever. Their husbands too are worthy of my respect always. The story of the second birth of Daksa is told here as in this birth These sons-in-law of mine, viz. Vasistha, Atri, Pula- stya, Angiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhrgu and Marici are very great. She mentally retained the Agneyi Dharana. Fire came out of all limbs of her body and was blown by the wind, from the Agneyi Dkaraija. It reduced her to ashes. You are known as Vrsabha (a bull); you are honoured by the people; the moon and the sun are your eyes; Brahma is your heart; you are fire and water; you are the lord achievable by pious rites. O Siva, neither Brahma nor Visnu nor the ancient sages can understand your greatness precisely. Your subtle forms do not come within the ken of my vision. Protect me with them as a father does to his son. The Lord is always sympathetic and favourable to his devotees. And I am always devoted to you. May that lord be always my protector—the Lord w o after devouring (withdrawing at the time of Pralaya) thousands of men, abides all alone at the bottom of the ocean. nii., ' ~ b f Isaace to the Yogic soul whom persons of impartial Obeisance to them all, for ever, who do not cry and who, stationed in the body, make the living beings cry. Obeis¬ ance be to them who are delighted and who delight all. Perpetual obeisance to them, whc arc stationed in the ocean, in the river, in the fort, on the mountains, in the caves, at the roots of trees, in the cowpens, in the dense forests, in crossroads, in the streets, in the quadrangular courtyards, in the assemblies and in the midst of the sun and the moon, in the rays of the sun and the moon, who have gone to the nether- worlds and beyond them. Perpetual obeisance to those who are subtle, gross, lean or short. O Lord, you are all in all; you pervade all; you are the lord and the inner soul of all living beings. Therefore you were not invited to the sacrifice. Since it is you alone who are worshipped with sacri¬ fices with various monetary gifts and since you alone are the doer of everything, you were not invited. O Lord, I was deluded by your subtle Maya that you were not invited. O Lord ofDevas, be pleased with me. You alone are my refuge, my goal, my foundation. I have no other goal or resort." After eulogising the great lord thus, the Prajapati stopped. The delighted lord spoke then to Daksa: "O Daksa of good rites, I am pleased with this hymn of vours; of what avail is much talk. You will come near me. Then the lord of the three worlds, conversant with the appropriate use of words spoke consoling words and said
30.10: "O Daksa, you shall not be angry due to this hind¬ rance. It is I, none else, who destroyed the sacrifice. You have seen that before. O you of good rites, again, accept this boon from me. With your face beaming with delight, you shall listen to me with attention. O Prajapati, by my grace, you will derive the merit of a thousand Asvamedha and a hundred Vajapeya sacrifices. Having established the Vedas with their six an- cillaries together with the Samkhya and Yoga and performmg O blessed one, you shall derive the bench 1 - of this holy rite. May your mental worry be over." After saying thus to Daksa, the valorous lord vanished along with his consort and his followers. O Brahmanas, after obtaining his due share as men¬ tioned by Brahma, the lord who was conversant with the holy rites, divided Jvara (fever) into many classes 1 for achieving calmness in living beings. Listen to it. For elephants it is excessive pain in the head; for mountains it is bitumen; for waters it is the bluish tinge; and in serpents it is the slough. It is Khour aka (cracks in the hoofs) for all cattle. It is banenness for the earth. O Knower of Dharma! to the ele¬ phants it is the obstruction to vision. It is the opening of pores to the horses, the splitting of the crest to the peacocks, the ailment of the eyes to the It is splitting 6f the bile to the goats. It is Himika \?) O Omniscient lord, it is fever to the human heiners It He who reads the story of the origin of Jvara with un¬ dejected and concentrated mind shall be freed from the ailment. He will rejoice, attaining all joys in accordance with his desires. lie who nairates or listens to the hymn of praise re¬ cited by Daksa, attains longevity. He will never face inauspicious results. Just as Siva endowed with Yogic power is the excellent of all Devas, so also this hymn of Brahma is the excellent of all hymns. The lord shall be eulogised with devotion by those who desire fame, kingdom, happiness, prosperity, riches, longevity, wealth and learning. The sick, the distressed, the indigent, the frightened, those afraid of thieves and those on the king's errand are liberated from dangers. He will attain all happiness here itself. He will become the chief of Ganas with this body itself. In a house where the lord is eulogised, neither the Yaksas nor the Pis'acas, neither the serpents nor the impediments create obstacles. A celibate woman who listens to this with devotion will become the object of respect of the families both from her father's and her husband's side. The affairs of the man who constantly listens to or narrates all these will become fruitful without impediments. By the repeated recitation of this hymn, whatever he thinks in his mind and whatever he speaks out, will become realised. After offering oblations to the lord, Guha, Goddess and Nandlsvara, as far as he can, practising mental control and restraint of the sense organs and united in Yogic communion, he shall repeat the names of the lord in the proper order. He will attain his desires, ambitions and enjoy pleasures. On death he will attain heaven surrounded by a thousand women. One who performs undesirable activities or one who is defiled by sins becomes free from sins on reading the hymn So said the holy lord Vyasa, son of Parasara. This episode is a secret that shall not be divulged to anyone. After hearing this secret, even the sinners, whether they be Vaisyas, Sudras or women, will attain Rudraloka. The Brahmana who recounts this to the other Brahmanas during Parvau days attains Rudraloka. There is no doubt about this.

31.1: Thus the sin-destroying* story in the context of Daksa as told by Siva, has been narrated to you. In the context of describing the race of Pitrs, this story has been narrated. In succession to the Pitf$, I shall describe Devas hereafter. Formerly, in the Svayambhuva Manvantara, in the beginning of thcTretaage, there were Devas known as Yamas. They were formerly the sons of Yajna. Those known as Ajitas were Brahma's sons. Those known as Jitas and Jitajitas were the mental sons of Brahma. They were known as Sukras. There were three groups of Devas, namely (Yama, Sukra and) Trptimanta. They were the chanters of the Samaveda and were thirty-three in all in Svayambhuva Manvantara (or born of Brahma).
31.2: The Yamas are twelve in number, viz. Yadu, Yavati, Didhaya, Sravasa, Mati, Vibhasa, Kratu, Prajati, Visata, Dyuti, This chapter corresponds to Bd. P. 1.2.13.87-151. In addition to Devas, the chapter discusses the nature of Time etc. in w. 24 ff. In the Svayambhuva Manvantara a thousands of the offsprings of these passed away. They were endowed with pro¬ wess, beauty, longevity and vigour. They are not mentioned in detail so that no new topic be raised here. The creation of Svayambhuva should be under¬ stood (as similar to) the present Manvantara. The past creation should be seen through the present one, viz. Vaivasvata Manvantara in regard to progeny, gods, sages and Pitrs.
31.3: Now know the seven sages who existed before. They were Bhrgu, Angiras, Marici, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri and Vasistha. Svayambhuva Manu had ten valient sons, viz. Agnidhra, Atibahu, Medha, Medhatithi, Vasu, Jyotisman, Dyutiman, Havya, Savana and Putra. They have been mentioned by Vayu as kings of great valour in the first Manvantara. Their families, the Asuras, Gandharvas, Yaksas, serpents, Raksasas, Pisacas, human beings, Suparnas and groups ofApsaras-s cannot be enumerate in order, even in hundreds of years because the names are num¬ erous in their families. Those who were known by the name of Vrajakula and who were in the Svayambhuva Manvantara, passed away as much time elapsed in the order of Ayanas, years and Yugas. Who is this lord Kala, the annihilator of living beings? What is his source of origin? What is his beginning? What is his intrinsic essence? Who is his son? What is his eye? What is his form? What are his limbs? What is his name? Who is his Atman? Mention these in detail as we ask you. May the origin of the Kala be heard. After hearing it, may it be retained in memory. The sun is his source of origin. yimcsa is his beginning. He is called Sankhya-Cak?u (having Number as his eye).
31.4: His form is the day and night. The jYmesas are his limbs. A century constitutes his principle. Kala is his name. He is the Prajapati with the present, past and future as his Atman. Listen to the five divisions in which Kala is divided by means of days, fortnights, months, seasons and Ay anas. The first (year) is Sariivatsara. The second (is called) Parivalsara. The third is Idvaisara. The fourth is Anuvatsara and the fifth is Valsara. The group is called Yuga. 1 I shall explain their principle. Understand as it is being narrated. That which is mentioned as Kratu (sacrifice) and Agni (fire) is considered as Sariivatsara. 2 The fire of time which is the essence in the Sun-god is Parivatsara. He who quickens (lit. warms up) the worlds with his bodies seven times seven ( =49 Maruts) and who makes people to work actively (and quickly) that wind (god) is Vatsara.
31.5: He who while being born out of Brahma, roared thrice egotistically is Rudra. That Rudra who was born red-blue (in complexion) out of them is Vatsara. Now I shall explain to you their essential nature. Understand it as it is being narrated. Due to the contact of limbs and minor parts of the body (divisions and sub-divisions), the Atman of Kala is the great-grandfather. He is the source of origin of Rk, Saman and Yajus. He is the lord of all the five (viz. day, fortnight etc...). That (identical with) Yajus, Soma, Bhuta (elements) and Prajapati is called Samvalsara by learned men. And what is Agni but Sfirya (the Sun-god)? The Sun-god is the arranger of the divisions of time such as days, months, seasons, equinoxes as well as of the activities of planets, stars, of cold, heat, rain, span of life, holy rites, (but himself) is an evolute (being born of Brahma) of kindly disposition, the son of Brahma, the Lord protector of subjects. He is only one.* He is day, month, season and grand-sire (Brahma).
31.6: He is Aditya, Savitr, Bhanu, the enlivener of life, honoured by Brahma. He is called Bhaskara as he is the source of the origin and cause of destruction of all living beings and is hence designated as Bhaskara. The third Parivatsara should be known as the presiding deity of stars. As the moon is the Lord of medicinal herbs, he is called the great-grand-father. He is the life-bestower of living beings. He meets their needs and preserves them. By. his rays he surveys the universe and sustains it. The moon is the source of the origin of Tithis (days of the Lunar fortnight), junctions of Parvans, the Full Moon and the New Moon. He causes the night and is the Prajapati with nectarine soul. Hence he is fatherly soma of the nature of Rk,
31.7: He causes the unified and simultaneous activities of the five units of the physical body, viz. the sense-organs, the mind, the intellect, the memory and power". He is the source of origin of fire, water, earth, the sun and the moon. Hence he is Prajapati. He is the soul of existing worlds. He is the great-grandfather. When medicinal herbs decline, the Lord is worshipped byDevas, the chief of whom was Prajapati and who seek fruits eagerly desired bythem. He is worshipped (by offering Purotfaia) in three Kapalas (pots known as Arribaka). Hence he is called Tryarhbaka. The (Vedic metres) Gayatri, Tristubh and Jagau are remembered (known) by the term Tryambaka. They are the sources of the origin of sacrifice.
31.8: It is remembered as Tri-Kapala as the Puroda§a offering consecrated for (achieving) three means by the repetition of those three metrical verses united into one and through their efficacy. Thus the Yuga as mentioned by the learned, is one consisting of five years. The samvatsara that has been mentioned by Brahmanas as one having five-fold selves became a set of six selves with the names of Madhu (spring) and otherseasons. The sons of the seasons are five. Thus this crea¬ tion is mentioned briefly. This wind (vital air) alone is the life of living beings. The destroyer Kala runs with the force of the current of a river with day and night for his hands. Hence he is called the wind. These are the Prajapatis (Lords of subjects) most im-
31.9: The lord manifested himself by coming outof the mouth of Brahma, as he was meditating. Hence he (the great lord) Mahadeva, the sage, the Brahmana, the soul of all living beings is the great-grandfather. He, the lord of all living beings is identical with the Pranava. The creation of the limbs (major and minor) of living beings is due to the entry of the soul (into the body). Agni, Samvatsara. the sun, the moon, the wind—Lord Rudra, the soul of Kala, the all-pervader always condenses these. It is called Idvaisara when it causes exhilaration and blesses the world. In this universe everything is penetrated and permea¬ ted by Lord Rudra with his own brilliance, bodies and names by the relation of the supporter and the supported.

Thus the lineage of Devas cannot be enumerated due to their multiplicity. Their sons and grandsons are too many to mention. He who glorifies this lineage of great Prajapatis of noble deeds and stable renown will attain great Siddhi.

34.1: On hearing of the establishment of the people, the clever and eminent sage asked Suta about the length and extent of the earth. O holy sir, how many continents, or oceans or moun¬ tains arc there? How many Varsas( sub-continents) are there and what are the rivers in them. Explain factually to us in details, the magnitude of the great elements and of the Lokaloka mountain, the circum¬ ference, the size and the course of movements of the sun and the moon.
34.2: Henceforth I shall explain the length and extent of the earth, the number of oceans and continents in details. I shall tell you how many countries ( Varfas ) there are and whatthe rivers (are) therein. (Now) I shall tell you the magnitude of the great elements, the Lokaloka mountain range, There are thousands of countries and islands in the seven continents. They cannot be described in details with sufficient evidence, even in hundreds of years.
34.3: One shall not make conjectures about inconceivable objects and worlds. That which is beyond Prakj-ti is called eternal. I shall describe to you factually Jambudvipa consisting of nine Varsas. Understand its extent and zones in Yojanas. It extends to a hundred thousand Yojanas. It is full of different rural localities and various splendid cities. It is embellished with the (colonies of) Siddhas, Caranas and Gandharvas and with mountains as well. It has mountains abounding in minerals and variegated rocks. It has many rivers rising from mountains.

They extend to both sides plunging into the eastern and The mountain Himavat is full of snow. Hemakuta is full of gold; Nisadha is golden having the lustre of the midday sun.
34.5: The golden Meru of four colours is known as the highest. 2 Leaping up in symmetrical shapes on all sides it rises up. On its sides it has various colours. It is endowed with the attributes of Prajapati. It is born of the umbilical knot of Brahma, of unmanifest origin. It is white on the east, hence its Brahmanahood. It is yellow on the south, hence its Vaisyahood.

39.1: Henceforth I shall tell you about the excellent abodes of Devas situated on different mountains.
39.2: The forest of sport of Mahendra is on the great mountain Sltanta. The forest is endowed with all desirable qualities. The mountain contains many belly-like caves, which are the abodes (of Devas). The mountain is very extensive with hundreds of variegated minerals and jewel mines. It is the abode of animals of good qualities. Its ridges and slopes are laden with flowers where the bees hum and buzz. It is decorated with the assemblage of gold pieces veriegated with valuable jewels. The slopes hum with the buzzing sound of bees. There are corals mixed with gold. The ridges are covered with flowers where the bees hum. There are hanging creepers of various colours. Hundreds of minerals are spread over the peaks and precipices. Gems of different colours along with flowers decorate the mountain. There are fountains and springs of pure and tasty water. It is embellished with many hedges abounding in flowers. It is beautified with streamlets wherein flowery rafts float. The inner crevasses of the mountain are frequented by Kinnaras. There are many caves and cavities frequented by Yaksas and Gandharvas. Some of them are comfortably resorted to and some are dense and impassable. Many animals frequent it. Good potable water is abundant. The mountain is embellished with trees bearing various fruits and flowers.
39.3: The great Parijata forest of the king ofDcvas is also there. It is well—known in the three worlds and is praised in song as can be ascertained from reports.
39.4: By means of the excessively fragrant and charming flowers blazing like the midday sun, the excellent mountain is illuminated as it were all around.

41.1: Kailasa is the abode of the devotees of the lord who are of meritorious souls. It has isolated, charming summits. It is full of vegetation. It has the lustre of the conch. This is a poetic description of the peak near Lake Manasa and not of the trans-Himalayan Kailasa range. The climatic conditions of those days. seem favourable for vegetation and human habitation.
41.2: In the central ridge, as beautiful as Kunda flower, there is the invincible city of the noble-souled Kubera, 1 the presiding deity of wealth. It is a hundred Yojanas in length and fifty Yojanas in breadth. It is beautified with a series of big mansions, set in diverse ways in gold and silver. It is very extensive, affluent and joyful. There is a charming assembly-hall in the centre, embe¬ llished with variegated pieces of gold. It is known as Vipuld be¬ cause it abounds in archways and pillars.
41.3: The aerial chariot Puspaka, decorated in jewels, is there. It is very charming and endowed with all desirable qualities. As quick as the mind, it can reach any desired goal. It is decorated with clusters of gold pieces. It is the vehicle of Kubera, king of Yak§as.
41.4: Lord Kubera the companion of Mahadeva lives there. He is the king of Yaksas revered and honoured by all living beings. Kubera, excellent among Devas, lives there along with Apsaras-s, Yaksas, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Caranas.
41.5: Here the Lord of Wealth has eight treasures: 2 Padma, Mahapadma, Makara, Kacchapa, Kumuda, Sankha, KJa and Nandana. 42.4: WhenSiddhas pass through the sky in their aerial chariots (great many in number), they have a sip in the sacred and healing water of this river.

43.1: Near Gandhamadana there is a large and bulky boulder above, thirty-four thousand Yojanas long, and thirty- two thousand Yojanas wide, east to west. The residents of this area perform auspicious rites. They are well-known as Ketu- malas. The men are black in complexion. They are vigorous and powerful. The women have the lustrous complexion of the petals of a lotus. All of them have pleasing appearances.
43.2: There is a great divine Panasa (Jack-fruit) tree there. It has six tastes. It is the son of Brahma, capable of moving about according to its pleasure. It has the speed of mind. It is veritable svara himself. Imbibing its juice, the people there live for ten thousand years.
43.3: Tiie men are fajr-complexioned, vigorous and powerful.
43.4: They have the complexion and lustre cf the moon and their faces resemble the full moon. Their bodies are as cool as tncmoon. They have the fragrance of lotuses.
43.5: Their span of ale is ten thousand years. They are free from ailments. Imbibing the juice of the black mangoes, they enjoy perpetual youth.
43.6: The magnitude, lustre and the span of life oT the people of all the four great continents have been explained precisely ancl succinctly, but not in detail.
43.7: O Sages of enhancing reputation! The characteristics of the people of Bhadrasva mentioned by me are what have been cited by earlier Siddhas. Now listen to them in detail.
43.8: I shall narrate fully and in detail what I have seen and heard, of the five principal mountain ranges, countries and rivers which surround the famous Devakuta mountain.
43.9: The five principal mountains are Saivala, Varnama- lagra, the excellent mountain Koranja, Svetavarna and Nila.
43.10: There are hundreds, thousands and crores of small mountains besides, which are offshoots of these five ranges.
