45.1: O holy lord, the two continents in the east and the west have been narrated to us. Now tell us about the people dwelling in the northern and southern continents as well as those on the mountains. South of the Sveta mountain and north of the Nila, there is a sub-continent called Ramanaka 1 where human beings are born. Animals (thereof) fulfill desires in all seasons. People are free from the stink of old age (They do not become senile or decrepit). They are a good-looking people descended from a noble, fair-complexioned race.
45.2: There is a great divine Nyagrodha tree (the Indian fig tree) called Rohina. The people subsist on the juice of its fruit. Those excellent people are always delightful and happy. They live for eleven thousand five hundred years. To the north of the Sveta and to the south of the moun¬ tain called Sriigavan, there is a sub-continent called Hiranyata 2 {Hiranvat in A) where a river Hairanyatl (Hairanvati in A) flows.
45.3: Identified with ancient Sogdiana (AGP 8S-84). This Varsa is closely associated with the river Hiranvati (mod. Zarafshan). Both forms of the name mean 'possessor or scatterer of gold*. Due to its association with this river, this Varsa must be presumed to be adjacent to Sogdiana—AGP 84-85. Very strong and brilliant men are born there who are Sattvic in quality, bestowcr of desires in all seasons. They are rich and comely in appearance.
45.4: These people of unlimited splendour live upto twelve thousand five hundred years. In that country there is the great Lakuca tree (Bread¬ fruit tree) yielding six tastes. Men maintain themselves on the juice of its fruits. There the Spigavan mountain has three great and lofty peaks. Out of them one is full (lit. consists) of diamonds, the second, of gold and the third, full of all kinds of precious stones. They are embellished with mansions.
45.5: On the southern shore of the northern sea is the holy country of the Kurus 1 which is resorted to by the Siddhas. The trees there provide sweet fruits and flowers throughout the year. They put forth clothes and ornaments along with fruits. Many are the charming trees that bear fruits desired by all. They exude excellent honey of exquisite taste, colour and fragrance.
45.6: There are other charming trees called ICsirin. They always yield milk like nectar yet presenting six types of tastes. The entire ground is full of jewels, even the fine sand being gold which is pleasant to touch. It is auspicious, free from impurities and thorns. Descending from the world of Devas, people are born as auspicious men. They are born in fair complcxioned families and have perpetual youth.
45.7: The charming women give birth to twins who imbibe the nectarine juice of the Ksirin (milk-yielding) tree. The twins are born simultaneously and grow up to- They have great vigour and vitality. They live upto fourteen thousand five hundred years. They never lesortto others' women.
45.8: North of Jarudhi, the king of mountains, are the north¬ ern Kurus. 1 he land is glorified in all directions. Now listen to its detailed description. There are two lofty Kula-Parvatas, Candrakanta and Suiyakanta. 1 They arc embellished by many caves, crevasses, cavities and rivulets; they possess many bushes and hedges.' They arc decorated with minerals of various colours. They con¬ tain many kinds of metals; they are adorned with all kinds of mineral ores. They have trees with perpetual fruits, flowers and roots; they are resorted to by Siddhas and Caranas. The whole of that country is pervaded by hundreds of their peaks and ridges. The great river Bhadrasoma 2 flows in between the two mountains, Candrakanta and Suryakanta.
45.9: There are thousands of other rivers with pure and tasty water, sufficient for the Kuru people for drinking. Similarly there are thousands of great rivers flowing with milk, honey, butter and the intoxicant beverage Maireya. There are hundreds of pools full of curds. There is a huge mountain rich in tasty food, nectarine, ripe fruits of diffe¬ rent kinds.
45.10: There are roots and fruits of sweet fragrance, taste and colour. Their fragrance can be smelt from a distance of five Yojanas. There are thousands of flowers of different colours and shapes, large, pleasant and conducive to welfare. There are forests ofTamala, Aguru and sandal-wood pleasant to touch and rich in fragrance, colour and taste.
45.11: The forests are in full bloom. Bees hum and hover round. The forests abound in pleasant trees, hedges and creepers. O excellent Brahmana, there are thousands of lakes abounding in lotuses and lilies wherein bees Hum and birds chirp. Identified with mod. Tarbagatai and Jingar—Ala Tau mountains.
45.12: Mod. Irtysh river. There are many charming grounds of sports afford¬ ing pleasure in all the seasons. There foodstuffs, garlands, un¬ guents, beds, seats and other articles of enjoyment are ever available. Birds of beautiful shape and variegated colours chirp there.
45.13: The grounds of sports are flourishing and richly em¬ bellished in gold and jewels. There are bowers and grottos of plantain and other trees as well as rocks. There are thousands of bowers of creepers all around They are very pleasant. There are hundreds of underground houses as lustrous and pure as conch shells. The windows are made of gold adorned with a net¬ work of diamonds. They are very large and of various sizes with wonderful workmanship in gold and gems.
45.14: There are thousands of excellent trees. The clothes are of various shapes (and fashions). They are of fine texture and very pleasant (to the sight). There are various musical instruments like Mrdanga, Venn, flute, Panava which are widely used. There are hundreds and thousands ofKalpa trees bearing fruits.
45.15: There are parks of that description everywhere and so They never grow old. They have perpetual youth. They are fond, affectionate and comely in appearance. They live upto many thousand years. They do not procreate nor do they decline in numbers. Pairs arc born of the tree unlike each other but befitting each other.
45.16: The riches arc common to all. They do not have the sense of possession. There is no virtue, no vice, no sickness, no old age, no mental confusion, no feeling of exhaustion. On completing their full length of time, they disappear like bubbles of water. They are extremely happy, devoid of all miseries. Be¬ ing passionately attached, they do not observe (the restrictions of) Dharma. For Dharma grows from misery.
45.17: To the southern side of Northern Kurus, there is the famous country called Candradvipa 1 shaped like the disc of the moon. It is at a distance of five thousand Yojanas beyond the region of gods. (Being a seaside land) it is ever decorated with garlands of sea waves and is resonant with many sounds. It extends to one thousand Yojanas in area and is full of fruits and flowers. It is fertile and flourishing. It is one hundred Yojanas in breadth and so much in height. There is an excellent mountain Kumudaprabha in its centre, inhabited by Siddhas and Garanas. It has various gems equal in lustre to the moon. These have all good traits and shine in their lunar shape. There are lilies of diverse colours, parks and gardens of variegated hues. There are many rivulets and caves. It is deco¬ rated with great ridges, precipices,.crevasses and bushy hedges. The excellent river of many waves, Candravarta flows from this mountain. It is full of pure and holy water, bright like the moon's rays.
45.18: There is the excellent abode of the moon, the lord of stars. The moon, the lord of planets, always resides there. There is a famous mountain known by the'name of the moon. The great land called Candradvipa is famous both in this world as well as in heaven.
45.19: The Tuva region in southern Siberia where the river Yenisi flows. All the people here shine like the moon. They resemble the moon, with their faces shining like the moon. They are free from dirt and consider the moon their deity. The people there, are very virtuous, gentle, truthful and brilliant. Their conduct is good and their span of life ex¬ tends to a thousand years.
45.20: To the west of this western continent is the land called Bhadrakara four thousand Yojanas from the ocean. It is a circular zone ten thousand Yojanas in diameter. It looks splendid with different kinds of flowers. The place is rich and abounds in foodgrains. It is ruled over by many kings. It is joyous, prosperous and beauti¬ ful on account of the great mountains.

45.22: With its diverse features giving rise to auspicious and inauspicious results, this sub-continent is in the middle, to the north of the ocean and to the south of Himavat. Since the country ( Var$a ) is called Bharata the people are Bharatls. Since Manu ruled over the people, he is called Bharata. 2 Etymoligically derived thus the Varsa (country) is called Bharata.

49.1: O excellent Brahmanas, I shall describe the Plaksa- dvipa 1 precisely but succinctly. Listen to it as I narrate it exaedy. Its extent is twice that of Jambudvipa. Its circumference (perimeter) is thrice its breadth. This briny sea is surrounded by that continent. The people over there are righteous -and have a great longevity. There is neither famine nor fear of old age and ailments.
49.2: The dvipa derives its name from Plaksa tree (a fig tree) (v. 26). It indicates Mediterranean climate V.V. Iyer identifies Plaksa with Greece and adjoining lands in 'The Seven Dvipas of the Puranas*, Quarterly Joum. of Mythic Society (London) XV. 62. 75. M. Ali identifies it 'without hesitation as the basin of the Mediterranean (AGP 41). Placia, a town in Mysia is traceable to Plaksa. There are seven mountains and seven rivers there also. They are splendid sources of precious stones. I shall mention their names. In the seven continents, Plaksa and others, there are seven great and steep mountains established in all directions.
49.3: I shall first mention the seven great mountains in the Plaksa Dvlpa. The first is Gomedaka resembling a cloud. The country too is named Gomedaka after the name of this mountain. The second mountain named Candra is full of medicinal herbs. For the preparation of Amrta (nectar) (gods) Asvini Kumaras planted the medicinal herbs here. The third is named Narada. It is an impassable mountain of great height. It was on this mountain that the sages Narada and Parvata were born.
49.4: The fourth mountain is called Dundubhi. On this mountain, formerly a drum was beaten by the Devas, the sound of which killed living beings. The Salmala tree by its drum Rajjudara full of ropes slays the Asuras. The fifth is named Somaka where the nectar was collected formerly by Devas. It was taken away by Garu<Ja for his mother. The sixth is named Sumanas and also Rsabha. The demon Hiranyaksa was killed by Varaha on this mountain.
49.5: The seventh mountain is Vaibhraja. It is great and I shall mention the names of the countries of these mountains in due order. The first country is Gomeda. It is a peaceful country (where fear is quelle.) e coun r Candra is Sikhara; that of Narada ». Sukhod>ya thatrf Dundubhi is Ananda; that of Somaka is Siva, th is Rsabha; and that of Vaibhraja is Dhruva., In these countries Devas, Gandharvas, i as >
49.6: The rivers flowing into the sea, in this con tmen, seven, one for each country. I shall mention the names of these rivers known as the seven Gangas. These rivers along with thousands of their tributaries flow (towards the ocean). They are always in flood with abundant water, as the rain-god Indra showers (rains) profusely. The people in these realms drink from these rivers and are delighted. The seven rivers are Subha, Santavaha, Pramoda, Siva, Ananda, Dhruva and Kemaka. There the people are righteous. They observe the duties and rules of their castes and stages of life.
49.7: They are all free from ailments. They are strong and never suffer from illness. Among them there is no (influence of) Utsarpirii (evolutionary) and Awssrptyi 1 (involutionary) eras. There is no division of time based on the peculiarities of the fourYugas. The condition of Trcta Yuga is perpetually prevailing there. In the five continents beginning with Plaksa, the activities of the seasons accord with those of the (particular) continent.
49.8: The people live for five thousand years. They are handsome, well-dressed, strong, and free from sickness. In the continents beginning with Plaksa and ending with Saka, happiness, longevity, strength, beauty, health and virtue are exquisite. Plaksadvlpa is large and glorious. It abounds in riches and foodgrains. It is endowed with divine medicinal herbs and fruits. It has many kinds of plants and herbs.
49.9: There are thousands of domestic and wild animals there. O excellent Brahmanas, the details of Plaksa Dvlpa are covered by the details of Jambu Dvlpa. (Just as Jarhbu Dvlpa is There also, in its countries, there are seven mountains and rivers. They should be known as sources ofprecious stones. The first mountain is named Kumuda. It is asrefulgent as the sun. Its peaks are rocky and abound in all minerals.
49.10: The second mountain there is famous by the name Unnata. It envelops die heaven by its peaks, full of yellow orpiment. The third mountain thereof is known as Balahaka. With its peaks of collyrium, it stands enveloping the sky. The fourth is named Drona 1 2 where the strong medici¬ nal herbs Visalyakarani (remover of darts or splinters) and Mrtasanjivani (that which re-suscitates the dead) are found.
49.11: The fifth mountain is Kanka of excessive height. It is covered with trees and creepers endowed with divine flowers and fruits. The sixth mountain is Mahisa resembling clouds. A fire, bom of water and known as Mahisa, exists there. The seventh mountain is called Kakudman. Indra himself showers innumerable gems there. This is the procedure to be performed in Prajapatya rite in honour of Prajapati.
49.12: There are seven mountains in the Salmala Dvipa.They are bedecked in jewels. I shall now describe the seven auspi¬ cious countries ( Varsas ) associated with them. The first ( Varsa) is Sveta connected with mount Kumuda, and the second is Lohita connected with Mt. Unnata. The Varsa associated with Balahaka and Jimuta and that with Drona is Harita, that of Kanka is Vaidyuta, that of Mahisa and that of Kakuda is Suprabha. These are the seven countries and their seven mountains. Now know the rivers there. From its description in vv.. 29-45, M. Ali identifies it with tropical Africa bordering on the Indian Ocean, including Madagascar A
49.13: Mount Droria is noted for its medicinal plants. VR vi. 50.31 locates it in Ksirasagara. De (p.58) identifies it with mount Doonagiri in Kumaun while it is located here in the Salmaladvipa (land of silk cotton trees). Pani, Toy a, Vitrsna, Candra, Sukra, Vimocanl and the seventh (river) Nivrtti are the rivers of their respective countries. There are hundreds and thousands of adjacent rivers which cannot be enumerated. They are to be believed (taken for granted) by one who wishes to know them.
49.14: Thus the locus of Salmala Dvipa has been described to you. Like the great Plaksa tree in Plaksa Dvipa, there is a Salmali (silk-cotton) tree in the middle of the Dvipa which is named after it. It is surrounded by the ocean of wine equal to Salmala fdvipa) in extent. O knowers of Dharma, now listen to the description of the people in the northern continents. Understand as I relate to you in accordance with what I have heard. I shall describe the fourth continent Kusa Dvipa 1 succinctly. The ocean of wine is surrounded on all sides by this continent (Kusa).
49.15: It is twice the extent of Salmala. There are seven mountains there. Listen as they are being described to you. The first mountain in the Kusa Dvipa is known as Vidrumoccaya; the second is Hema; the third is Dyutiman, a mountain resembling clouds; the fourth is Puspavan; the fifth is Kusesaya; the sixth.is Hari; and the seventh is Mandara. The word Manda means waters and Mandara means that which splits the waters. The distance between these mountains is twice their magnitude. The first country is Udbhida; the second is Venumantfala; the third is Svairathakara; the fourth is Lavana; the fifth is Dhrtimat; the sixth is Prabhakara; and the seventh is Kapila. These are the seven countries and mountains.
49.16: In these Varsas Devas, Gandharvas, Prabhas, Prajapatis are seen residing and sporting about. In these countries there are neither robbers nor Mlecchas. The people are mostly fair in complexion. They die according to seniority in age. Here also are the seven rivers which are auspicious and which dispel sins. The chief of them are Pavitra, £>antati, Dyutigarblia and Mahl.
49.17: Hundreds and thousand of others arc known as their The Kusa Dvipa is surrounded by the ocean of ghee. In extent it is equal to Kusa Dvipa. Thus the position of Kusadvlpa has been described to you. Now I shall explain the extent of Kraunca Dvipa. 1
49.18: It is remembered to have twice the area of Kusa Dvipa. The ocean of ghee is encircled by this continent. In this continent the chief mountain is Kraunca. The next after Kraunca is Vamana and the next after Vamana is Andhakara. After Andhakara comes Divavrt. After Divavrt comes Divinda.
49.19: After Divinda is the great mountain Pundarlka. After Punqlarlka is the mountain Dundubhisvana. These are seven bejewelled mountains of Kraunca Dvipa. They abound in fruit trees and a number of creepers. The Varsa mountains are twice in height as compared with the previous ones. Now I shall mention the names of the

49.22: I shall henceforth explain the features of the entire Saka Dvipa 1 exactly as they are. Listen as I recount them precisely. Its extent is twice that of Kraunca Dvipa. It encircles the ocean of whey. All the countries there are very sacred. People die only after a long life. There is neither famine nor fear of old age and sickness.
49.23: There also are seven bejewelled mountains which as well as the rivers are the sources of gems and precious stones. Listen to their names. The first mountain, called Udaya, extends to the east. It is golden and is the abode of divine sages and Gandharvas. Hence it is like Meru. Clouds rise and pass pouring down showers. There is a great mountain Jaladhara where Indra showers plenty of water. There in the rainy season people get ample showers.
49.24: There is mountain Raivataka raised by god Brahma. It is here that the Star Revati is always established in the heavens. Beyond that there is a very great mountain called Syama. It was due to it that people got dark complexion from the outset. Next is the massive mountain Astagiri, full of silver.
49.25: Next to Ambikeya is Ramya where all medicinal herbs grow. It is called Kesarl and the winds blow on it. M. Ali identifies this with the monsoon lands of Asia where teak abounds, viz. Malaya,Siam, Indi-China (AGP 39), while De(np 172-173) identifies it with Tartary including Turkestan in central Asia. Listen to the names of the countries of* these mountains in due order. The country (Var S a) of the mountain Udaya is Udaya well known as Jalada. The second Varsa, that of Jaladhara is Sukumara; that of Raivata is Kaumara; that of Syama is Mamcaka, the splendid Varsa of Asta is Kusumottara; of Ambikeya is Modaka; and that of Kesaras is Mahadruma. '
49.26: The extent, magnitude, length and breadth of this continent are as those of Saka dv!pa(?) A great tree called Saka (teak) grows in its centre and is worshipped by the people. Devas, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Caranas are visible and play about here in the midst of people. The people (in the countries thereof) are virtuous and observe (the distinctive rules of) their respective four castes ( Varnas ). There are seven rivers flowing to the sea, one in each Varsa and these seven rivers are remembered as the seven streams of Ganga.
49.27: The first river is known by the names Sukumari, Ganga, Sivajala; and Anutapta, the second is known asKumari, Siddha and Sati; the third is designated as Nanda and Parvatl. The fourth is Sivetika which is also remembered as Tridiva; the fifth is known as Iksu as well as Kratu. These seven great Gangas of auspicious waters sanctify all the people residing in Saka dvipa every year.
49.28: There are thousands of others rivers joining them. They have abundant of waters since Indra showers rain profusely. It is impossible to enumerate their names and magnitudes. These excellents river are very holy. The joyous people drink from them. ' O Samsapayana, this continent is very extensive. It is like a wheel, covered by rivers and cloud-like mountains wonderful and variegated with minerals and decorated with jewels and corals. The cities are of various shapes. They abound in flourishing and prosperous people.
49.29: The continent is full of trees laden with, flowers and fruits. It is flourishing with wealth and foodgrains. It is sur¬ rounded by the ocean of milk equal in size to it. The land-tracts amongst those mountains are seven in number. They are holy and splendid. The people there¬ of abide by the rules of castes and stages of life and adnut no They arc neither greedy nor deceptive and neither jealous nor malicious. There is no loss of fortitude nor adverse results. Everything is natural with them.
49.30: No tax is raised. No punishment is meted out. There is none to punish. They know of virtue by natural righteousness. They protect one another. This much and no more can be mentioned about the The ocean of milk is surrounded by Puskara Dvipa, 1 which is twice the Saka Dvipa in extent.
49.31: There is only one glorious mountain called Mahasila having lofty peaks full of variegated jewels. This great mountain with wonderful and variegated ridges and precipices stands in the eastern half of the Dvlpa. Its circumference is twentyfive thousand Yojanas. Its height is thirty-four thousand Yojanas. The excellent Manasa mountain encircles half this Dvlpa. It stands In fact the two mountains constitute but a single mountain with peaks and ridges divided into two. It is surroun- ded by the ocean of fresh water.
49.32: In the two countries [Varsas) the forms and features and the span of life are similar. There is no distinction of high and low among them. In appearance and conduct of life all of them are equal. None defrauds (anyone); none is jealous. There are neither thieves nor fear nor imprisonment nor punishment, nor greed nor illegal acceptance of gifts. There is neither truth nor falsehood nor virtue nor evil nor the rules of caste nor the stages of life. There is no trade, no cattle breeding, no business enterprise.
49.33: The lore of the three Vedas, the system of civil and military administrarion, acts of service to others in return for payment, wounding others with harsh words or sharp im¬ plements—these are absent in the two Varsas of Puskara. There are no rivers, no rainfall, neither bitter cold nor oppressive heat, no vegetation, no water, no mountains, no rivulets. The season is perpetually the same as in Northern Kurus. The people are happy, devoid of old age and exhaustion. This is the condition in DhatakI and Mahavxta countries. Thus Puskara is surrounded by the ocean of sweet water equal in extent to that continent.
49.34: The seven continents are encircled by the seven oceans. The ocean immediately adjacent to a continent encircles it. The relative increase in the size of the continents and oceans should be known thus. Since they have abundant increase of waters, the oceans are called Samudras. The word Rsi is derived from the root VRf- The root WVrs means the continuance of energy. Since the land-tracts afford continuance of energy they have the designation
49.35: In the bright half, when the moon waxes, there is A Popular etymology of Varfa -'a continent'. In the bright fortnight, the ocean gets filled with water by itself. In the dark fortnight, the ocean recedes bv itself. Just as water in a cooking pot boils up b y its contact with fire, similarly water in the vast ocean swells in quantity and magnitude.
49.36: The increase and decrease of water is of fixed qua¬ ntity, neither more nor less in the bright and dark fortnights at the rise and setting of the moon. The increase and decrease in the ocean again is the result of the waxing and the waning of the moon. It is observed that the increase and decrease of (the level of water in) the ocean is upto five hundred and ten angulas. This (increase and decrease) is seen (occurring) on the parvan days. The term dvipa (island) is so called on account of waters being on either side. 1 They are surrounded on all sides. As it is a store-house of waters, the ocean is called Udadhi.

49.38: In the above-mentioned two sub-continents of Puskara Dvipa, god Brahma himself protects the subjects who are (as if) adorned with good people. The supreme ruler Brahma, the lord of. three worlds, holds the rod ( Dantfa) of chastisement (to govern them). He is their lord, Visnu, Siva, father and grandfather. 49.42: The.infiniteUnmanifest (Prakrti) is subtle and divided into ten. It is infinite, immobile (with no Soul). It has neither beginning nor end. It is beyond everything. It is terrible. 49.43: Verses 152£T c i ve p - • From Patala to heaven there is a fivefold course. This is the extent of the Universe. This is the ocean of the worldly existence. i he activity of the Universe with neither beginning nor end goes on like this arising from different types and groups of people. This unsteady activity of the Universe is really wonderful. The physical creation of this is very extensive. It cannot be comprehended even by the blessed Siddhas who know things even beyond the scope of sense-organs.
49.44: O excellent Brahmanas! There is no limit, decline or end to the magnitude of (the elements, viz.) Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Mahat> Tamas > the infinite, omnipre¬ sent Lord Isvara. While enumerating the names of the Lord (Siva), I have mentioned this before. The Lord who is called by the name Siva has been glorified to you. He pervades everything and is worshipped in He is to be realized through penance as the Lord of great splendor. This great God, the great Yogin has divided himself in various forms. He, the Lord of the worlds, is worship¬ ped in various ways in all the worlds.
49.45: Thus the worlds orginating from one another support one another by the relationship of the supporter and the suppor¬ ted or as the effects of their cause. The elements earth etc. are the evolutes covered up by one another. They enter into one another, the lesser into the greater. Since they penetrate one another, they have attained stability. Formerly they were without special features. But by intermingling they became possessed of speciality. e eZT > fire and the wind, these three are separately and accurately Their accurate ascertainment is specially noticed by the decline in attributes and essence. The accurate determin¬ ation of the rest is not observable due to their subtleness.
49.46: Aloha is beyond all the Shiites (elements). They are discernible separately only in the illuminated Ether (Akaia\. Just as in a big vessel smaller vessels are placed and are mutually supported by it though separate from each other, similarly the separateness of the elements is internal within the illuminated Ether (Akasa). All these four elements are consecutively bigger, the later bigger than the former. The creation can function as long as the elements exist.
49.47: The perfection (creation) of creatures is regarded as being within (i.e. based on) Bhutas (elements). The creation of effects cannot take place without Bhutas. The Bhutas being of the nature ofeffectsare restricted. The entities e.g. the Mahat (Cosmic Intellegence etc.) are of the nature of causes. Thus, O Brahmanas, the arrangement of this earth with seven continents and oceans has been explained to you along with their divisions precisely as they are. The cosmic form of Pradhana (the Unmanifest Nature) which has been described (lit. enumerated) to you by its extents and zones, is only a partial modification. Its cosmic form is the abode of the Lord to whom belongs the whole Universe. In this way, the elements have interpenetrated each other.
49.48: Only this much of established arrangement (of the Universe) can be explained by me. O King, only this much need be heard in regard to the constitution and arrangement of the world. The seven Prakrits support one another. There are many Prakrits above and below and on all sides. I shall explain them to a little extent. O excellent Brahmanas, now I shall describe the position of the luminaries, the boundaries, the horizon and sub-horizon of the earth.

50.1: Water is present in rivers, oceans, small receptacles such as ponds or puddles, mountains, firmament and the bowels of the earth. Hence water should be regarded as infinite. Simi¬ larly, the element of fire pervades all the worlds. It is said to be infinite, all-pervasive and born of everything. In this way there is no end to the evolutesof the Bhutas. They are infinite. Know that this has been decisively mentioned by gods formerly. The sequence should be known thus. First the earth, then the water and the sky thereafter. This ordei pievails upto the seventh world—Rasatala. The nether world extends 1 to ten thousand Yojanas at each rung. Each of these rungs has been explained in detail by the sages.
50.2: The first rung is Atala, below that is Sutala. The widely extensive Vitala is below that. Thereafter come Gabhastala, Mahatala, Srltalaand Patala is known as the seventh. The ground surface * of the first (nether-world) is black; of the second, pale white; of the third, red; of the fourth, yellow; of the fifth, sandy, gravel-covered; of the sixth, rocky; and of the seventh, golden. In the first nether-world, there stands the palace of the lord of Asuras, Namuci, the enemy of Indra. The following abodes too are in the first nether-world, viz. the abode of Maha- nada, the city of Sankukarna, the palace of Kabandha, Ni§-

50.4: In the fifth Nether-world that is covered with sand and full of gravel extending to many Yojanas, there is the city of the intelligent Daitya chief Virocana, the lion among Dait¬ yas, the abodes of Vaidurya, Agnijihva and that of Hiranyaksa, the city of the intelligent Vidyujjihva, the lord of Raksasas, the city of Mahamegha, that of Malin, the leading Raksasa, the city of the serpent Karmara and those of Svastika and Jaya. In the sixth Nether-world, there is the excellent city of Kesari, the lord of the Daityas, the cities of Suparvan, Sulo- man and Mahisa, and the city of the noble-souled Utkrosa, the leading Raksasa. It is there that Satasirsa the son of Surama, lives joyfully. The king of serpents named Vasuki, the son of Kasyapa (stays there). It should be known that the city of Bali is in the seventh and the last Nether-world, Patala. It is beyond every world. It is gay and full of men and women.
50.5: It is full of Asuras, serpents and teeming with haughty enemies of the Devas. There itself is the great city of Mucu- kunda, the Daitya. It is teeming with innumerable great cities of Daityas, full of bustle and commotion and thousands of the rich and prosperous city of the serpents. It is crowded with great rising (flourishing) cities of Daityas and Danavas and the many flourishing abodes of Raksasas. O leading Brahmanas, at the (lowest) extremity of atala extending to many Yojanas, lives the excessively brilliant e§a, king of all serpents. His eyes resemble a red lotiis. He is noble-souled, free from death and old age. His complexion is w ite as the interior of a shining conch-shell. He wears blue garments. His arms are mighty. His body is large and expansive.
50.6: Thus the seven Nether-worlds that could be discussed have been recounted. They are always inhabited byDevas, Asuras, great Serpents, and Raksasas. Beyond this is total absence of light. It cannot be traversed by Siddhas and Sadhus (good people or sages). It is unknown even to Devas and is traffic (life)-less. O excellent Brahmanas, thus is the grandeur of earth, fire, water, wind and ether described by the sages. There is no doubt about this.
50.7: I shall now describe the rotation of the sun and the moon. 1 These are stationed in the ether along with their discs and shine with their lustre as long as they move. 50.8: Now I shall mention the magnitude of the moon and The extent of Bharata is equal to the extent of the vastly extensive disc of the sun. Now listen to the number of Yojanas it covers. The extent of the sun is nine thousand Yojanas. The girth or the extent of its disc is thrice its diameter. The lunar disc is twice the solar disc (in diameter as well as girth).
50.9: Now I shall recount the extent of the earth in Yojanas. The extent and girth (circumference) of the earth consisting of seven continents has been reckoned in proper mea¬ sure in the Puranas. I shall recount that after enumerating the current Abhimanins (Deities etc. who preside or have the sense of possession etc.). Those Abhimanins who have gone were on a par with the current ones. The Devas who have gone are on a par with, the current ones in forms and names. Hence, I shall describe the surface of the earth through the current Devas. (I shall recount) the situation of the heavenly world entirely through the current (Devas). The entire earth is known as fifty crores (of Yojanas) in extent. From the middle of Meru on all four sides is half
50.10: Half the extent of the earth is stated in terms of Yojanas. The extent of the earth towards all the sides (quarters) from the middle of Meru is said to be eleven crores and eighty- nine lakhs (of Yojanas) and fifty thousand * 2 ). It is considered as the radius of the circular zone. The sphere at the extremity is thrice this in extent. On being calculated thus the spherical zone of the extremity of the earth has the overall area of eleven crores one hundred and thirty-seven thousand Yojanas. Thus the measurement upto the extremity of the earth has been specified:
50.11: The outer surface of the globular sphere of the earth is co-extensive with the sphere of the stars in the firmament. In regard to the magnitude of the outer surface the firmament is equal to the earth. The same is the measure of all the seven worlds. The worlds arc situated above oneanother spreading like an umbrella with their outer spheres. They are all populat¬ ed. Thus the cauldron of the Cosmic Egg has been explained. These seven worlds shaped in the form of umbrellas are severally supported by their own subtle outer coverings, which are ten times bigger in order. They are created with specific attributes and they support the seven worlds.
50.12: All round this Cosmic Egg there is a solid ocean. The entire sphere of the earth is supported by the solid water. 1 Beyond the solid ocean is the solid fire by which the sphere of the world is supported. Beyond and outside the solid fire is the sphere of solid wind that covers the earth on all sides round and above. Beyond the solid wind is the firmament which is surrounded by Cosmic Ego entirely. That Ego is surrounded by Mahat (the Great Principle or Intellect) which again is surrounded by the infinite Unmanifest Prak r ti of un¬ changing form. I shall enumerate in order the cities of the guardians
50.13: This Puranic concept of seven protective sheaths of our Cosmic Egg shows the influence of Sankhya Tattoos. To the east of Meru and above Manasa is the holy city of Mahendra abounding in all essential riches and richly inlaid with gold. To the south of Meru and above Manasa lives Yama son of Vivasvan, in his city Samyamana. To the west of Meru and above Manasa is the charm¬ ing city of the intelligent Varuna. It is called Sukha.
50.14: To the north of Meru and above Manasa is the city Vibhavari of Soma (the moon) which is comparable to the city of Mahendra. Above Manasa in all the four quarters the guardians of the worlds are stationed for the establishment of virtue (Dharma) and protection of the worlds. Understand the solar movement when the sun reaches south during the southern transit all round above the guardians of the worlds.
50.15: In his transit to the south, the sun moves fast like a discharged arrow. It takes the group of luminary bodies with it and revolves always. When the sun is in miclday in Sukha, the city of Varuna, it rises in Vibhavarl, the city of Soma. It is midnight in Amaravatl and the sun sets in the city of Yaraa. Then the sun is in midday in Vibha, thecitv of Soma. When the sun rises in Amaravatl, it is midnight in Samyamana and the sun sets in the city of Varuna. Making the stars (and planets) whirl and revolving itself like a fiicbiand, the sun sots and then rises quickly.
50.16: Thus the sun moves in the four continents ending with the southern one. It rises and sets again and again. The sun gives warmth to two abodes of Devas in the forenoon and two in the afternoon. With its rays alone it heats one of them during midday. After rising the sun blazes with its rays of increasing heat till midday. Thereafter with its rays of decreasing heat it sets.
50.17: Where the sun appears rising, it is known as sunrise to the people thereof; (while) where the sun vanishes, it is called sunset in regard to the people there. Due to the far distant position of the sun and being covered up by the line (horizon) of the earth, its rays become invisible (being obstructed from sight). Hence it is not seen at night. The appearance of the planets, stars and the sun as well as their rising and setting should be known by the magni¬ tude of their height. Fire and water have white lustre and the earth ha? black shadow. Since the sun is at a great distance at the time of rising, it appears to be without rays. Since it is without rays, it has the red lustre, and the absence of heat is due to its redness.
50.18: Wherever the sun is seen to be stationed on the line (of horizon) it is seen a thousand Yojanas above. When the sunsets, the brilliance of the sun partially enters fires. Hence fire shines more brilliantly at night, even from a distance. When the sun rises again, the brilliance of fire enters the sun. This together with the brilliance left in the sun at the time of sunset, makes it all the more brilliant. So the sun blazes during the day.
50.19: The light and heat of the sun and fire getting mixed together nourish people during day and night. In the northern and southern halves of the earth when the sun rises, night enters waters. Hence, during day waters are copper-coloured as a result of the entry of night. When the sun sets, day enters waters. Hence during night, water appears white and bright as a result of the entry In this manner, in the southern and northern halves of the earth, day and night enter waters at the time of sunset and sunrise.
50.20: Day is the time when there is sunlight and night is the time when there is darkness. Hence, night is established (independently) due to this, while day is dependent on the sun. When the sun passes through the middle of the sky, it traverses one-thirtieth of the diameter of the earth in a Muhurta (forty-eight minutes). In regard to the distance traversed in Yojanas, f a! 111 1S three million one hundred and fifty thousand in lull. This is the distance traversed by the sun in one Muhurta.
50.21: The extent of the zone in the northern quarter in Yojanas as calculated by the Brahmanas is one crore eight million and fiftyeight Yojanas. The northern orbit is called Nagavlthl 1 and the southern one is called Ajavlthl. When the sun rises in the constellations Mula, Purvasadha and Uttarasadha it is called Ajavlthl. When the sun rises during the rise of the three stars after Abhijit (i.e. Asvini, Bharani and Krttika) it is called Nagavlthl. I shall mention the distance in Yojanas between these two quarters. This distance is three million one hundred and three thousand three hundred and thirtythree Yojanas. Now I shall mention the distance between the south¬ ern cardinal points and meridians in Yojanas. Understand it.
50.22: The magnitude of this zone is twentyone thou¬ sand two hundred and twentyone Yojanas. This is the measure¬ ment of the zone calculated in Yojanas. The diameter of the zone is laid obliquely. Everyday the sun traverses those (zones) indue order. Just as the outer rim of the potter's wheel comes back (revolves) quickly, so also the sun returns quickly during its southern transit.
50.23: According to Varahamihira's B r hat-Samhitd, Vithi is a particular division of the planetary sphere comprising of three astensms. Thus Naga- vlthi is constituted of asterisms Asvini, Bharani and Krtti a w i e javi formed of Mula; Purvasadha and Uttarasadha. Tlie sun passes through tliirtccn and a half constella¬ tions of stars during the day. During the night in eighteen Muhurtas it passes through as many (i.e. thirteen and a half) of stars. Just as the central region of the potters wheel moves slowly, so also in the course of the northern transit the sun moves slowly. The sun passes through thirteen and a half stars. Hence it covers less extent of the earth in longer time.
50.24: In the later part of the northern transit, a day has the duration of eighteen Muhurtas. Then also the sun proceeds very slowly. The sun passes through thirteen and a half stars dur- ing half the time (i.e. the daytime). During night, it passes through as many stars in the course of eighteen Muhurtas. Just as a ball of clay placed on the middle of the wheel whirls slowly, so also does the Pole Star.
50.25: They say that day and night together constitute thirty Muhurtas. The whirling Pole between the two quarters revolves in a circle. Just as the nave of the potter's wheel remains there only, similarly it should be known that the Pole Star whirls there only (without changing its place). Thus the rotation of the sun in a circle between the two quarters is slow during day and fast during night. During the northern transit, the movement of the moon (?) is slow during day and fast during night.
50.26: Dividing nights and days thus by its special diverse movements, the sun traverses the path by its even (regular) and uneven (irregular) movement. 50.27: There is as much of sunlight at the sides, behind and all round Lokaloka as there is on its top in front. This mountain is above ten thousand Yojanas in height. It ispartlybright and partly unilluminated. It is circular all round. The stars, the moon, the sun and planets shine within the internal part of mount Lokaloka. The world is only so far and no further. Beyond this there is darkness. The Lokaloka is single but Niralokas (the darker sides) are numerous.
50.28: Since the sun in its circular movement unites the Lokaloka, the wise call the inter-space between Usa and Vyusti by the name Sandhya. Usa is night and Vyusti is day. A curse was cast on the wicked demons who were bent on devouring the sun at the time of twilight that they would have imperishability of bodies but they would be made to die (everyday). Three crores of demons who are well-known as Mandehas seek everyday the rise of the sun. The wicked ones harass and desire to devour the blazing sun.

As the water became adamantine, the Daityas were burnt. Then the sun of great splendour, excessive lustre and valour rises up a hundred thousand Yojanas. Then goes forth the Lord (the Sun-god) with his bril¬ liant rays. He is surrounded by Brahmanas and Valakhilya Sages who have achieved their object (of protecting the Sun). 50.38: Its eastern peak in the middle is golden. The south¬ ern peak consists of silver. It has crystalline lustre. The excellent peak in the north consists of precious stones and jewels. Thus with the three peaks the mountain is well known as Srngavan. Betwixt autumn and spring, the sun proceeds with medium velocity, neither fast nor slow. 50.39: Divine green-coloured horses are yoked to his great chariot. They appear (shining) as though they are smeared with the (solar) rays red like lotus. During the Mesa and -Tula zodiacal transit of the sun days and nights contain fifteen Muhurtas beginning with sunrise. When the sun is in the first quarter of the constella¬ tion Krttika (Pleiades), the moon is known to be in the fourth part of the constellation Visakha. 50.40: The sages call that as equinox. Equinox shall be known through the (position of the) sun and the time through (that of) the moon. When days and nights are equal it is equinox. During equinoctical transit oblations to the Pitrs and charitable gifts to the Brahmanas should be made. Brahmanas are the mouths of Devas. 50.41: The six months, viz. Magha, Phalguna, Caitra, Vaisa- kha, Jyestha and Asadha are the months oWttardjana (northern transit of the sun). The six months, viz. Sravana, Bhadrapada, Asvina, Karttika, Margasirsa and Pausa are the months of Dcknnayana (southern transit of the sun). These months make a year. The five years are the sons of Brahma. Rlus are born of them. These are their parts. Hence the New Moon Day (Amavasya) is known as the leader of the Parvans. More than that the equinox should be known as favourable to Devas and Pitrs. After knowing this, a man should not get deluded regarding rites concerning Devas and Pitps. Hence equinox is remembered as all-pervasive by the people.
50.42: The worlds (Lokos )should be known (toexist) as far as light (the space illuminated by the sun) extends. The end of the world is also called Loka (of the Lokaloka mountain). The guardians of the worlds are stationed there in the middle of the Loklaoka mountain. They (the Lokapalas) are the four noble souls who stay till the final dissolution of the world. They are Vairajaof good (brilliant) splendour, Kardama of good and merciful dis¬ position, Parjanya of golden hair, and Ketuman of fixed deter¬ mination. The guardians of the worlds are stationed in the four •quarters in Lokaloka, free from Dvanduas (mutually clashing opposites), devoid of arrogance, without an attendant, and absolutelyuncontrolled by anyone else.

According to Nirukta XI-29, Pauqiainasi (the full moon day) when. mixed with the 14th Tithi, is Anumati and when mixed with the 1st day When Amavasya (the new maon day) is mixed wit., the 14 h Tithi, it is Sinivali and when mixed with the 1st Tithi of the next(i.e. bright) fortnight it is Kuhu. Stationed there in the path of Pitryam are the sages blessed with progeny who perform Agnihotras and who perpe¬ tuate the lineage of the world.
50.44: Desirous of the welfare of the worlds, they bless the activities of living beings and begin the activities of Rtviks. Theirs is the southern path. In every Yuga they re-establish Dharma that has gone astray (being rudely shocked and shaken) by their progeny, penance, adherence to the bound of decency and persuit of learning. The earlier ones on their death are reborn in the houses of the later ones. This series of births and deaths makes them live upto the hour of final dissolution of the universe.
50.45: There are eighty thousand householder-sages re¬ sorting to the path south of the sun. They stay there as long as the moon and the stars exist. In view of their worldly activities, the creation of living beings, natural desires and hatred, sexual intercourse and other sorts of enjoyments of pleasures as well as due to other causes, the Siddhas have resorted to cremation grounds. These sages, desirous of progeny, were born in the Dvapara age. The path north of Nagavlthi and south of the Sapta Rsis (Great Bear) is Devayana, the northern path of the sun. The Siddhas residing there are unsullied and celibate. They hate sexual intercourse. They have conquered death. These Ordhvareias sages (who have sublimated their sexual desire) are eighty thousand in numbers They have re-, sorted to the northern path of the sun and stay there till the final dissolution overtakes the universe.
50.46: In view of these pious causes they have attained deathlessness that will last as far as the final dissolution of the Bhutas (elements). Deathlessness is predicated of those who survive till final dissolution. This is the period (of life) till the three worlds last, for sages who do not return to the path of Samsara. Others of To the north and above the world of sages, where Dhruva is said to be present, is the divine shining region of Visnu, On reaching that region none is affected by sorrow or pain. It is the greatest region of Visnu where Dharma, Dhruva and other Sadhakas of the world stay.

51.1: While narrating the details of Svayambhuva Manvan- tara, events of past and future have been narrated. Now I shall recount them in their proper order.
51.2: On hearing this, the sages asked Lomaharsana about the movements of the sun, the moon and the planets.
51.3: How do these luminary bodies revolve in the firma¬ ment? They all move in circular orbits and laterally. Still they do not collide with one another. Who makes them revolve?Or do they revolve of their own accord?
51.4: O excellent one, we wish to know this. Narrate it to us. This is a matter that deludes living beings. We have a desire to hear about this.
51.5: Listen to and know this wonderful thing which though very clear and visible, deludes people.
51.6: It is Dhruva, son of Uttanapada, who is stationed at the tail-end of what appears like the Gangetic porpoise with tails
51.7: It revolves itself and makes the sun and the moon revolve along with the planets. While it revolves like a wheel, the stars follow it.
51.8: The group of stars moves at the will of Dhruva. 2 The sun, the moon, the fixed and moving stars and the planets are bound to Dhruva through the bonds in the form of groups of winds. It is from Dhruva that their combination, difference, seasonal movement, rising and setting, portentious phenomena, southern and northern transit, the equinoxes and colours begin to function.
51.9: Rain, heat, snow, night, twilight, day and the auspicious
51.10: The sun covers the stars etc. activised by Dhruva and stands by. Hence his rays are illuminated. The sun is the deadly fire (that ends the world).
51.11: O Brahmanas, in the course of his revolution, the sun brightens the quarters by his brilliance. With the mass of his rays in the company of the wind all round, O excellent Brah¬ manas, the sun takes up the waters of the universe.
51.12: The water drunk in by the sun gets transferred to the moon from the solar fire. Through the Nadis (tubular veins) full of wind the activity of sustaining the worlds begins.
51.13: What exudes from the moon, the sun receives at its tips. When the wind blows the clouds let it shower on the earth.
51.14: Thus the water is poured and it falls again and again. The same water assumes various shapes. 3
51.15: For the up-keep of the living beings, Maya has been created. The three worlds including the mobile and immobile beings are pervaded by this Maya.
51.17: Bh. P.V. 23.2 attributes this driving power to Kala (Time).
51.18: This belief in indestructibility of water is surprisingly modern, though the concept of water-cycle is archaic.
51.19: J h<; su. n " the lord of the universe; he is the creator of the worlds; he is the thousand-rayed lord; he is the lord of the subjects; he is the sustainer of the world; he is lord Visnu him- self.
51.20: The water of the worlds has exuded from the moon in the sky. The universe is, therefore, supported by the moon. This fact has now been declared.
51.21: The hot rays emanate from the sun; the cool rays from the moon. These two powerful hot and cool rays sustain the universe.
51.22: The holy Gariga with pure waters has the moon for support. O excellent Brahmanas, the great rivers have the son of the moon as their leader.
51.23: Water is present in the bodies of living beings. When the bodies of the mobile and immobile beings burn, the water becomes vapour and rises on all sides. Thereby clouds arise and they arc the receptacles of water. The brilliance of the sun takes up the water from the living beings through the rays.
51.24: The rays take the waters from the ocean through the wind. The revolving sun imparts water to the clouds by means of his white rays in the proper seasons.
51.25: When blown by the wind, the water drips from the clouds. The clouds scatter showers for the benefit of living beings when they are blown by the winds in all directions.
51.26: The clouds shower for six months in order to nourish and develop all living beings. They produce the rumbling sound of thunder arising from the wind and brilliant lightning arising from the fire.
51.27: The root s/mih means 'to exude', 'to sprinkle'. Since the clouds exude water, they are called Alegha. That from which water does not fall off they call Ablira. 1
51.28: Clouds arise in three ways. Their source of origin arc three. The types of clouds are Agneyas, Brahmajas and Paksajas.-
51.29: Abhra from.y/Umriu is a fanciful derivation. It is usually derived from \Zabhr 'to wander about* + suffix ac (i.e. <x) or from ap+i/bhf +s
51.30: Clouds arising from the waters of ocean are Agtiejyas. They function therefrom. Chilliness and winds on a cloudy day are their attributes.
51.31: They assume the shapes of buffaloes, boars and elephants in their rut. They roam about and sport very near the
51.32: The clouds are called Jimutas since they are the source of living beings. They do not have the attributes of thunder. They hang down due to the water-content in them.
51.33: These clouds are huge and silent. They follow the current of the wind submissively. They shower water within a half to one Krosa (from the earth).
51.34: They shower on the tops and ridges of mountains and sport. They pierce the wombs of the flocks of the white cranes. They make them conceive.
51.35: The types of clouds called Brahmajas are born of the breath of Brahma. They have the attribute of lightning. They are fond of rumbling sounds. They thunder.
51.36: Due to their loud report the earth gets a thrill. Like a queen crowned by a king earth attains youth once again. Being the cause of the birth of the living beings, the earth endears itself to the clouds.
51.37: The birth of living beings is from these clouds called Jimutas. These clouds resort to the second layer of wind called Pravaha.
51.38: These clouds shower from a distance of a Yojana, half a Yojana or one-fourth of a Yojana from the earth. They rain in continuous torrents.
51.39: The wings of the powerful mountains who could go as per their will and pleasure, had grown very large. Indra cut them off for the (welfare of all) living beings.
51.40: These clouds are called Puskaras. They are huge and they are exhilarated with their waters. For that reason they are called Puskardvartakas (revolving Puskaras).
51.41: They assume different forms. They are very terrible.
51.42: The third type of clouds mentioned before shower at the close of the Yugas. They assume many forms and fill the
51.43: All the clouds are reputed to have been born of the same Cosmic Egg-shell of Prakfta form from which the self-bom four-faced Brahma was born.
51.44: It is the smoke that makes them all fully developed without any difference. The most excellent among them is Par- janya. And there are four elephants of the quarters.
51.45: Elephants, mountains and clouds along with serpents belong to one and the same family, though they are severally manifested, since water is known as the source of (their)
51.46: During Hemanta (early winter) Parjanya and the elephants of the quarters born of chilliness shower snow (drops) for making the corn flourish.
51.47: The great wind called Parivaha is their support. It is that lordly wind which sustains the Ganga that flows through the sky. ' It is the sacred, heavenly river, flooded over with water, stationed in the heavenly path like the divine Lore (Vidya).
51.48: The elephants of the quarters spray all round drops of water from the Ganga by means of their huge trunks. That (spray of water) is called the hoarfrost.
51.49: Controlled by Dhruva, the sun causes the rainfall through these two (types) of clouds. The wind encompassed by Dhruva withdraws the rain.
51.50: The wind starts from the planet sun and traverses the entire stellar zone. At the end of the day it enters the sun en¬ compassed by Dhruva.
51.51: Now listen to the description of the Sun's Chariot. 1 It has one wheel with five spokes and three naves. The Lord Sun goes ahead on his Chariot that has golden wheel, that is very powerful, that has knotty joints, that has six-fold rim and one felly, which dispells darkness on the way.
51.52: This Chariot had been made by Brahma for some specific purpose. It is divine and golden. Swift horses have been yoked to it.
51.53: It is the Vedic metres that have assumed the forms of the horses. It is stationed in the sphere ofSukra (Venus). It has the characteristics similar to those of Varuna's chariot. In this shining Chariot the Sun traverses the sky. These parts of the Chariot of the Sun are fashioned out of the parts of the year in due order.
51.54: The day is the nave of the wheel. The Chariot has one
51.55: The Kasthas constitute its nose and the Ksanas (mo¬ ments) make up the shaft; the Nimesas are the axle-trees and the Lavas make up the poles. The night is the frontal fender; Dharma is its highly nsing banner. Artha and Kama are the two tips of the pole and
51.56: Verses 54 ff. give a symbolic description of the Chariot of the Sun.
51.57: The se en Veche metres, viz. Gayatrl, Tristup, Anu-?tup, Jagati, Pankti, Brhatl and U?nik, have assumed the forms of horses and bear the burden. The wheel is fixed to the axle and the axle is fastened to Dhruva. The axle turns along with the wheel; Dhruva turns along with the axle. Urged by Dhruva the axle turns along with the wheel.
51.58: This is the description of the peculiar construction of the chariot. By means of the parts joined together a shining chariot is fashioned out.
51.59: With that the lord Sun moves quickly in the hea¬ ven. There are two reins of the chariot tied to the tips of the pole and the axle. Propelled by Dhruva the chariot moves in the sky in a circular fashion. Handled by Dhruva the tips of the pole and the axle on the right side of the chariot appear like white reins in a chariot of two wheels.
51.60: The two rays (reins) follow the whirling Dhruva. The tips of the pole and axle of the chariot are wind-waves.
51.61: Just as the rope tied to a peg revolves, in all direc¬ tions, so the two rays (reins) shrink in the zones in the Uttarayana. They increase in the Daksinayana. The two reins handled by Dhruva lead the Sun. When these are dragged by Dhruva, the Sun takes the internal revolutions.
51.62: The Sun thus traverses the one hundred and eighty circular zones of the two quarters. When the reins are released by Dhruva, it revolves round the external zones. Encircling them the Sun moves fast round the zones.

52.1: That chariot is occupied by the Devas, Adityas, Sages, Gandharvas, Apsaras-s, Gramanis (Yaksas), Serpents and Raksasas 1. The following reside in the Sun in succession for a period of two months each 2. Among them (gods) Dhatr, Aryama, (sages) Pulastya, Pulaha the Prajapati, the Serpents (Nagas) Vasuki and Sanlurnara, (Gandharvas) Turhburu and Narada, the foremost among the singing Gandharvas, the Apsaras-s Kratusthall and.Punjikasthali, Gramanis or Yaksas Ratha- kfcchra, Taporya 3 (?), Raksasas and Yatudhanas Heti and Praheti—these reside in the Sun during the months of Madhu and Madhava 4 (i. e. Caitra and Vaisakha). [These are the months in the season Vasanta (the Spring) ] The sublime concept of the Solar Chariot is based on Vaj.S. 15.15- Here Devas, Sages and Gandharvas represent light and immortality—the actinic portion of the Solar Spectra. The Serpents, Gramanis (Yaksas) and Raksasas signify heat or death, the thermal field of the Spectra. This Heptadofthe Sun signifies the mutual difference in the different "wave¬ lengths" of the seven colours. This may be regarded as Puranic VIBGYOR.
52.2: Verses 2-26 enumerate the names of the different Devas, Sages etc.— the heptad who occupy the Solar Chariot every two months. These verses are common to other Puranas such as the Mt. P. Ch. 125, Bd. P. 1.2. 23.2.24. The Vedic names of these occupants of the Chariot are' somewhat different. 'Rathaujas' in Bd. P. 1.2.23.2-5. During the months of Suci and Sukra (i.e. Jyestha and Asadha)., the months of the season grisma (summer), the following, reside in the Sun: (gods) Mitra, Varuna; (sages) Atri, Vasistha; (Nagas) Taksaka, Rarhbha; (Apsaras-s) Menaka, Sahajanya; Gandharvas Haha and Huhu; Gramanis (Yaksas) Rathasvana and Rathacitra; and Yatudhanas (Demons) Pauruseya and Dhava (Vadha in Bd. P.). Then during the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya (i.e. Sravana and Bhadrapada) the (following) other deities reside in the Sun: (gods) Indra and Vivasvan. So also (sages) Angiras, Bhrgu; the two Nagas Elaparna and Sankhapala; (Gandharvas) Visvavasu and Ugrasena, Pratah and Aruna; Apsaras-s Pramloca and Nimloca; the Yatudhana Vyaghra; and the Naga Sveta.
52.3: During the autumn, in the months of Isa and Orja (i.e. Asvina and Karttika) noble sages and deities occupy the Sun: (gods) Parjanya and Pusan; (sages) Bharadvaja and Gautama; Gandharvas Visvavasu and Suiabhi; the two Apsaras-s of auspicious characteristics Visvaci and GhrtacI; the famous Serpents Airavata and Dhananjaya; the leaders of armies and Gramanis Senajit and Susena; and the two Yatudhanas Apa and Vata. During the two months of Saha and Sahasya (i.e. Margasirsa and Pausa), the two months of early winter, the following reside in the Sun: (gods) Arhsa and Bhaga; the sages Kasyapa and Rtu; the two Senanis and Gramanis Tarksya and Aristanemi; the two fierce Yatudhanas Vidyut and Sphurja; and the Nagas Mahapadma and Karkotaka; the two Gan¬ dharvas Gitrasena and Ornayu; and the splendid Apsaras-s Urvasi Durine the two months of late winter the following The twelve sets of seven deities (heptads) identifyng themselves with their place of residence augment the excellent splendour of the Sun with their extra refulgence.
52.4: With well-known hymns of prayer the sages eulogise the Sun. Gandharvas and Apsaras-s attend upon him with dance and music. The Gramanis, Yaksas and Bhutas collect hideous and terrible things. The Serpents bear the Sun and the Yatudhanas follow him. Worshipping the Sun from the time of rising, the sages Valakhilyas lead him to the mountain of Sunset. The Sun blazes with his brilliance and in accor¬ dance with the prowess, penance, Yogic power, truthfulness, righteousness and strength of these deities. These stay with the Sun for (a period of) two months. They arc the (sets of seven): the Sages, Devas, Gan¬ dharvas Serpents, groups of Apsaras-s, Gramanis and most of the Yaksas and Yatudhanas.
52.5: On being glorified, these blaze, rain, shine, blow, create, and dispel the inauspicious demerits of living beings. They remove the auspicious merit of the wicked people and in some cases remove the sins of mobile beings. They are seated in the celestial aerial chariot. They go as they please. They have the velocity of the wind. They revolve along with the Sun and follow him throughout the day. Showering rains, blazing and delighting people, they protect living beings till the end of Manvantara.
52.6: By means of the ray (Susumna), the Sun develops the Moon in the bright half (of the month) day by day and it is complete (full on the full-moon days). Devas imbibe its nectar during the dark half. Thus he propitiates Devas with the nectar. After being sucked thus, the moon has only two Kalas (digits) left. Pitrs take it as Kavya offering. Devas and Saumyas consider it as nectar and drink it. Men conquer (satisfy) hunger by means of foodstuffs, beverages and medicinal herbs developed by means of rains, with water lifted up and released as rain-showers by means of his rays by the Sun, For half a month Devas are propitiated through nec¬ tar. For half a month Pitrs are propitiated by Svadha food. The Sun sustains human beings perpetually through food. The Sun sustains them through his rays.
52.7: The Sun moves ahead in his chariot of green horses. Through his rays he takes up waters. At the time of their release he discharges them. Thus the Sun sustains the mobile and immobile beings perpetually. He is carried by green horses. By means of his thou¬ sands of rays he drinks water. While being carried by green horses he showers it again. Thus the Sun moves ahead quickly in his celestial sphere by means of his single-wheeled chariot dragged by the unim¬ paired gentle horses. In the course of a day and night he traverses over the world of seven continents and oceans by means of his single- wheeled chariot dragged by the seven horses.
52.8: The Vedic metres that have assumed the form of horses are yoked to the chariot near the wheel. They can assume any form they please. They are yoked but once. They have the un- limited speed of the mind. They (are accompanied) by tawny coloured masters expounding the Brahman (or the Vedas). They cover one hund¬ red and eighty zones within one year. The Sun is eulogised by the sages through well-known words of prayer. He is served by Gandharvas and Apsaras-s by means of songs and dances. The lord of the heaven, the Sun thus traverses by means of his horses. The Moon too moves among the stars that stay in the pathway of heaven (vlthx). The increase and decrease of its rays are similar to the increase and decrease of the Sun.
52.9: The chariot of the Moon has three wheels. 1 The horses are tied in pairs on either side. The chariot along with the horses and the charioteer has come out of the womb of the waters. The threewheels have a hundred spokes. Excellent white horses have been yoked thereto. They are ten in number. They are slender and divine. They are unimpeded and have the velo¬ city of the mind. They are yoked but once (in the beginning of the Kalpa) and they travel till the end of the Yugas. A white serpent acts as therein in that chariot. All the horses are of the same colour. They carry the conch-coloured Moon. The names of the ten horses are—Yayu, Trimanas, y. r?a > Jf j ' ivala ' Ha y a = y araa, Turanya, Harftsa, Vyomin and Mrga. They carry the Moon till the close of the day(?) The gentle Moon goes ahead surrounded by Devas and Pitrs. In the beginning of the bright half when the Sun is m front, the interior of the city of the Moon is filled duly every¬ day The Sun develops the Moon drunk by Devas in the declin¬ ing ortnig t. The Moon is drunk for fifteen days and the Sun
52.10: Verses 50-83 describe chariots etc. Mercury (Budha) and others. Beginning with the second day in the dark half and ending with the fourteenth day Devas drink the watery wine, the nectar of the Moon that is essentially made up of water and that by nature consists of tasty essence. By the brilliance of the Sun the nectar is collected and prepared in the course of a fortnight. On the full moon night Devas, Pitrs and the Sages attend the Moon facing the Sun. The digits being drunk decline gradually in the dark half and become refilled in the bright half.
52.11: When days pass on gradually Devas drink the Moon for half a month until the new-moon day and go away. On the new-moon day Pitrs resort to the Moon. When the fifteenth part of the digits is left over in the later part of the day, that part is used up by the groups of Pitrs. The remaining digit is drunk by Pitrs during the period of two Kalas. From the lunar rays the nectar of Svadha comes out on the new-moon night. They drink the nectar and remain content for a month. They attain immortality. All these (following) are Pitrs: Saumyas, Barhisads, Agnisvattas and Kavyas. The years, which are enumerated by Brahmanas as five, are Kavyas. Saumyas should be known as Rtus (Seasons) and Barhisads are remembered as Masas (Months). Agnisvat¬ tas are Artavas (Fertility period?) and these are the creations of the Pitrs, O Brahmanas.
52.12: When the digit is being drunk by Pitrs on the fifteenth night i.e. Amavasya, the last digit is left and it is re¬ filled. The increase and decrease of the Moon are on the six¬ teenth day (at the beginning of each next half). Thus the in¬ crease' and the decrease of the Moon are caused by the Sun. I shall now mention the increase and decrease of the stars and planets; and also describe the chariot ofRahu later. The chariot of the son of the Moon (Budha, The chariot resembles cloud. It has the frontal The chariot of Bhargava ( Venus) is glorious. In refulgence it resembles the Sun. It is yoked with excellent horses born of the earth and having various colours. They are white (tawny), brown, blue, yellow, red, black, green, spotted and variegated. All the ten are highly blessed. They are not lean. They have the speed of the wind.
52.13: The chariot of Mars is glorious and golden. It is yoked with eight red, unimpeded horses. They are born of fire, and they can go everywhere. (Mars) traverses the signs of zodiac in straight, curved and circular lines. Then the scholarly preceptor of Devas, Bjrhaspati (Jupiter) of the family of Angiras, moves ahead in his golden chariot yoked with red horses. Eight horses as speedy, as the wind and divine in nature, are yoked to it. In a constellation this planet stays for a year; then he traverses quickly. Sanaiscara (Saturn) rides in a chariot made of black iron and traverses slowly. His horses are variegated in colour. They are born of the ether. Rahu's chariot is of Tamasic nature (dark-coloured). Eight black horses, as speedy as the mind, are yoked to it.
52.14: Leaving the Sun, Rahu rushes at the Moon during the lunar Parvan (i.e. the Full-Moon). Leaving the Moon it rushes at the Sun during the solar Parvan (i.e. the New-Moon day). Horses yoked to the chariot of Ketu are eight. They are as speedy as the wind. They have the colour like smoke from burning straw. They are strong. They are tawny (and variegated in colour) like donkeys. These horses of the planets I have explained along with their chariots. They are fastened to Dhruva by gaseous- rays. Being fastened by invisible gaseous rays, these (planets) being whirled, revolve in an orderly manner.
52.15: Being bound to Dhruva, the Moon, the Sun and the planets move about in the firmament. The planetary system united to Dhruva follows it as it whirls. Jusc as a boat is carried along by the water in a river, so the abodes of Devas are carried by the gaseous rays. Hence all the groups of Devas are seen in the firmament by everyone. 1 here are as many gaseous rays as there are stars. They are tied to Dhruva. They whirl Dhruva and whirl by themselves. Just as oil-crushers whirl and cause the wheel (of an oil-mill) to whirl, so also do the luminaries fixed (to Dhruva) on all sides by gaseous rays (bonds). They move about like a fire-brand on being urged by the whirling wind. Since the wind bears the luminary bodies, it is called Pravaha.
52.16: Thus the cluster of the luminary bodies united to Dhruva traverses the firmament. The Gangetic porpoise-like appearance in the sky made up of the stars is Dhruva. If it is seen in the night, the sin committed during the day is quelled. Persons looking at Dhruva regularly live for as many years, or even more, as there are stars in the "Gangetic porpoise" in the firmament. 1 This permanent Gangetic porpoise shall be realised in its various divisions. Its upper jaw is known as Uttanapada. Its lower jaw is Yajna. Dharma resorts to the top of its head. Narayana abides in its heart and Asvins stay in its forelegs.
52.17: Varuna and Aryaman are its hind thighs. Samvatsara is its penis and Mitra resorts to its anus. In its tail are Agni, Mahendra, Marici, Kasyapa and Dhruva. The four stars (?) and the Gangetic porpoise do not set. The stars, Moon, Sun, planets and constellations stay in the sky with face up or in front. They are in the form of a wheel. These are presided over by Dhruva. They circum¬ ambulate Dhruva which acts like the pivotal peg in the firmament. Verses 91-95 describe the heavenly Gangetic porpoise with various stars forming parts of its body.

53.1: Hearing this the sages became doubtful. They asked Lomaharsana again for its clarification. Sir, you have mentioned the famous abodes of Devas. How are these abodes? How are these luminaries? Please describe.
53.2: Please say everything precisely about luminaries. I shall explain to you what has been mentioned by great intellectuals of perfect knowledge, in connection with the origin of the Sun, the Moon, how the Moon and the Sun are the abodes of gods.
53.3: Now I shall mention the origin of three fires 1: celestial, elemental (atmospheric) and terrestrial. When the great night came (lit. dawned) on Brahma, born of the Unmanifest, the universe became undefined and enveloped by nocturnal darkness.
53.4: Vedic Aryans regarded Agni (Fire-god) as a great deity and it was given designations according to its functions. Puraias amplified the tradition and attributed cosmic functions in verses 5-18. Heating being the common factor between the Sun and fire, they are in a way identified. The credit of creating seasons through the rays of the Sun is given to Fire-god also. Only four elements were there. That which blazed at first is called terrestrial fire. The fire that blazes in the Sun is called Suci (celestial).
53.5: I shall now mention the characteristics of the fire called Vaidyuta (atmospheric) fire. Three fires—Vaidyuta (lightning), Jathara (gastric) and Saura (solar) are born of the womb of waters. Hence by drinking water the Sun blazes in the sky with his rays. The fire from lightning that burns trees cannot be quelled by water. Nor the fire in human bellies can be quenched by it.
53.6: The fire existing in the belly is full of rays. It is a great fire. The diffused light of the Sun devoid of heat is white and spreads everywhere. It partially (with its quarter part) enters the fire at night, when the Sun sets. So the fire is seen blazing from a distance.
53.7: The heat of the fire permeates the Sun when he rises again. With a quarter of the heat the terrestrial fire blazes forth. The light and heat of the Sun and fire develop by day and night, thanks to this mutual permeation.
53.8: In the northern or southern hemisphere, when the Sun rises, the night enters the water. Hence the water becomes copper-coloured during the day, because of the entry of the night. When this Sun sets again, the day enters the water. So during the night the water sparkles due to the entry of day.
53.9: That which blazes in the Sun drinking the waters through the rays is the celestial fire mixed with the terrestrial one. The celestial fire of a thousand rays is circular and shaped like a jar. With its thousand rays it takes up the water of the rivers, oceans, wells, desert lands, both mobile, i.e. flowing, and stationary. The Sun of golden form has a thousand rays that exude rain, chillness and heat.
53.10: Four hundred of those rays having variegated forms shower rain. The rays that generate rain are called Vandanas, Vandyas, Rtanas, Nutanas and Amrtas. Apart from these, there are three hundred rays that exude chilliness. These are called Drsyas, Medhyas, Vahyas and Hradinis.
53.11: These are called Candras. All these rays are yellow- coloured. He gratifies human beings through medicinal herbs; the Pitrs by means of Svadha;and Devas by means of nectar.
53.12: During spring and the summer he blazes with the three hundred rays. During rains and autumn he generates rain by the four (hundred rays). The Sun creates mist and fog by means of the three (hundred rays) during early and late winter. He deposits energy on the medicinal herbs. By means of Svadha he propiti¬ ates Pitrs. By means of nectar of three varieties he bestows immortality.
53.13: Thus thousand rays of the Sun achieve the purpose of the worlds. They differ according to the season by exuding water, chilliness and heat. Thus the bright and sparkling solar zone is described. It is the support and source of origin of the stars, planents and the Moon. All these, the stars, the Moon and the planets should be known to have originated from the Sun.
53.14: The Moon is the lord of stars; the Sun is the king of planets. The remaining five planets are known as Isvaras having forms as they please. It is said that the fire is Sun and (the source of) water is the Moon. Now listen to the source of other planets as explained in detail.
53.15: The commander-in-chief of the army of Devas, Skanda, is said to be the origin of Angaraka (Mars). Those who have perfect knowledge know that Narayana is the origin of Lord Budha. Lord Rudra himself who is the prototype of Dharma, the son of Vivasvat, in the world, is the origin of the great planet Saturn, the slowest of all planets. He is the most excellent among Brahmanas.
53.16: The two great planets with bright rays are Sukra (Venus) and Brhaspati (Jupiter), the preceptors of Asuras and Devas. They are the sons of Prajapati. There is no doubt that the' entire universe, all the worlds including Devas, Asuras and human beings, have their roots in the Sun.
53.17: It is his universal splendour, O leading Brahmanas, that shines as the refulgence of all heaven-dwellers such as Rudra, Indra, Visnu and the Moon. He is the Atman of all, the lord of all the worlds. He is the primordial great deity. Everything originates from him and merges in him.
53.18: O Brahmanas, the creation and dissolution of the worlds arose from the Sun formerly. The Universe is known as a planet. The Sun is the most excellent and refulgent planet. From him are born again and again and into him merge after death, all the moments, Muhurtas, days, nights, fortnights, months, seasons, years, sets of five years and Yugas.
53.19: Their time-calculation is impossible without the Sun. Without time there is no sacred scripture, no initiation, and no daily routine. Without him how can the seasons be named and clas¬ sified? How can the foodgrains and plants grow? How can there be medicinal herbs of good quality? Without the Sun, the thief of water, the scorcher of the Universe, all the affairs of Devas here and in heaven cannot go on.
53.20: O excellent Brahmanas, he alone is Kala (Time) and fire. He is the twelve-souled Prajapati. He blazes the three worlds including mobile and immobile beings. He alone is a mass of splendour. He is the entire world and benefactor of all the worlds. Resorting to the uppermost path of Vayu, he blazes this Universe by means of his splendour at the sides, above and below.
53.21: Seven among the thousand of the Sun already The Sun's ray called Susumna develops the declining Moon. It is said to be exerting power laterally and from The ray Harikesa is said to be the primordial cause
53.22: The sixth ray Arvavasu is the source of origin of Brhaspati (Jupiter). The ray Svarat develops Sanaiscara (Saturn). Thus all the planets, stars and constellations flourish by the energy of the Sun. The entire Universe too flourishes thereby. The Naksatra-hood (i.e. the term Naksatra) is so called due to (fact that) they do not decline. 1 2
53.23: The Sun too is a Naksatra because he falls into their Ksetras (spheres) and then by means of his rays he takes them The constellations ( Tarakas) are so called because they have crossed (the ocean of existence) by means of merit, be¬ cause [they resort to the planets at the end of their pious actions. They are called Tarakas because they enable others to cross (the ocean of existence) and because they are sparkling. Verses 45-49 trace the origin of planets to the specificfays of the Sun.
